<meta>This page marks the beginning of Section XII in the second volume of "Zend-Avesta." Fechner is synthesizing his metaphysical system, clarifying the relationship between the individual, the soul of the Earth, and the universal God.</meta>

## XII. Religious-Practical and Poetical Point of View.

Our teaching is thus briefly this: human spirits belong to a higher spirit, which binds everything earthly into one, and this spirit belongs to God, who binds the whole world into one. <note>Fechner is describing his "Day-View," a philosophical system where the universe is a conscious hierarchy: individual souls are nested within the larger soul of the Earth, which is itself nested within the infinite soul of God.</note> The spirit of the Earth, however, does not stand as a partition between us and God, but is merely the <term>mediation<note>original: "Vermittelung"; the bridge or connecting process.</note></term> that incorporates us into God himself in a specific way (Vol. I, p. 45), while we always receive the most general, highest, best, and most important things only directly from the whole of God and can seek them only in Him (Vol. I, p. 360, 373). 

Thus, we always remain entirely God's own. But our evil is not to be attributed to God; for God is the Whole, and we are only parts, <term>fractions<note>original: "Brüche"; suggests that individual beings are broken or incomplete segments of the divine totality.</note></term> of Him, and one cannot attribute to the Whole that which adheres only to the individual as such. Evil exists only in the lower realm of individual beings, the individual wills within God; it is not present through God's higher will, but rather this higher will exists in opposition to evil, and the <term>business of God<note>original: "Geschäft Gottes"; refers to the ongoing divine labor or cosmic task.</note></term> is to uplift and heal it in the course of time (Vol. I, p. 396 ff.). All of nature is animated by divine spirit, and just as our spirits—

<summary>Fechner explains that human souls are part of an Earth-spirit contained within God, and argues that evil arises from individual parts of the universe rather than God's supreme will, which works to heal such imperfections over time.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s argument from the previous page, where he suggests that just as our spirits are parts of a higher soul, our physical existence is part of a larger divine whole. He is addressing potential religious objections to his "Day-View," specifically the fear that seeing God as part of nature diminishes His majesty.</meta>

...only components of the spirit of the Earth and, further up, of the divine spirit, so are our bodies only components of the body of the Earth and, further up, of the divine body—of Nature.

But, you say, does it not remain, after all, a wicked doctrine, conflicting with religion and morality, that I should no longer place myself as an independent spirit over and against God, the most independent Spirit? That I should instead think of myself—regardless of whether there is mediation or not—as swallowed up by and within Him, like a limb in a body or a thought in a mind? To think of God as entangled in nature, instead of being <term>sublime<note>original: "erhaben"; often used to describe God as being "above" or "exalted" beyond the physical world.</note></term> above it?

I did not invent this doctrine; you yourself confess it in your religion. You simply do not believe what you confess; I, however, do believe it. This doctrine does not conflict with religion and morality; rather, the fact that you do not believe what you confess is what brings conflict into your religion and morality.

->Answer:<-

Do you not confess yourself that God is the <term>primal source<note>original: "Urquell"; literally the "original spring" or "wellspring" from which all life flows.</note></term>, the Creator of your spirit? But that which a spirit creates spiritually does not leave it; rather, the spirit manifests its activity within it. And if God creates spirits while we create only thoughts, He simply has spirits as His content—where we have only thoughts—within which He manifests His activity. How could He be God if there were no other kind of creation in Him than there is in us? Now, He creates lower spirits through the mediation of the higher ones. But even through the mediation of the higher ones, the lower ones still remain within Him. But let us set aside the mediations; only our

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s theological argument, moving from the previous page's discussion of God as a creator of spirits to the logical necessity of those spirits being contained within God. He is addressing a personified "opponent" to show that their own religious language supports his view.</meta>

Our relationship to God shall now concern us—that which exists immediately through all <term>mediation<note>original: "Vermittelung"; the idea that things might relate to God through intermediaries (like nature or other spirits) rather than directly.</note></term>.

And do you not yourself acknowledge, and consider it a beautiful saying, that God "lives and moves and works and exists" <note>original: "lebt und webt und wirkt und ist"; a phrasing common in German theology, echoing Acts 17:28: "For in him we live, and move, and have our being."</note> in you and in all things, and you in Him? But does one also live and move and work and exist within that which stands externally <term>opposite<note>original: "gegenüber"; a key concept for Fechner. If God is "opposite" us, He is limited by us. If we are "in" Him, He remains infinite.</note></term> us? What, then, still separates your doctrine from ours?

And do you not believe that for God, everything in your soul is clear and transparent down to the innermost depths; that He knows the most secret folds of your heart? But can one spirit also see clearly into a spirit that stands opposite it? Does the very nature of being "opposite" not consist in the fact that it cannot? Nothing of its own content escapes the spirit.

And do you not call God the only God, who has no other beside Him? But if there are still spirits that are not *in* Him, then He is not a unique One, but only a highest spirit among many. For surely there must be spirits higher than us. There we have <term>paganism<note>original: "Heidenthum"; here used to describe a polytheistic worldview where gods are separate, independent individuals rather than parts of a single divine whole.</note></term> with a highest spirit at the top and many beneath him, down to us. But you do not want paganism. Thus, you also cannot want a God who has us and spirits above us still *outside* Himself, but only one who has us all *within* Himself. Only that is a truly unique God, who encloses all the spirit that exists within His fullness, just as He brings it forth from it.

And do you not call God the infinite spirit, the spirit of the universe? But whatever still has something else opposite it also has its limit there; it still lacks something of the infinite fullness; yet to you, the concept of the infinite is almost still too small for God.

<summary>Fechner argues that for God to be truly infinite, unique, and all-knowing, all other spirits (including humans) must exist within Him rather than being separate or 'opposite' to Him. He suggests that the alternative—God as a separate being—results in a form of polytheism or paganism that his readers would reject.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s theological argument. Having previously established that spirits exist "in" God, he now appeals to the reader's own religious definitions—specifically God's attributes like omnipresence, love, and justice—to show that these concepts only make sense if the world and its inhabitants are part of God’s own being.</meta>

And is God not to you the **Omnipresent**, the **Omnipotent**, the <term>eternal ground<note>original: "ewige Grund"; in 19th-century German philosophy, this refers to the fundamental basis or underlying source of all existence.</note></term> of all that happens; His house the heavens; suns and stars pass through Him; no leaf falls from the tree without Him, and no hair from your head? <note>A reference to the words of Jesus in Matthew 10:29–30.</note> But does not heaven also encompass the earth, and you yourself with your body; must God then not also be omnipresent and omnipotent in all of nature and every creature, and must not all forces be His own and serve Him?

And do you not call God the **All-loving**, the **All-good**? But whose love and goodness could be greater than His, who cannot distinguish between the love He has for Himself and for His spirits; who, in what He does for them, does as if He were doing it for Himself? He cannot do otherwise, for He is truly doing it to Himself—only it is not that what He does for this one or that one, but rather what He does for everyone as a whole throughout the entire world is done unto Himself.

And is God not to you at once the **All-merciful** and **All-just**? But who would be more merciful than He who cannot even cast out the wicked, but holds him fast just as He does the good, and must turn his evil and his malice toward his own peace? And who, at the same time, could be more just than He—since evil is once here, who can deny it, even if it is evil only for us—who needs one evil to destroy another, turning the punishment against the sinner to <term>convert<note>original: "umzukehren"; literally "to turn around." Fechner suggests that punishment isn't for vengeance, but a necessary mechanical or spiritual correction to bring the individual back into harmony with the whole.</note></term> the sinner? Here or there, it must one day be accomplished, in order to fulfill His own inner satisfaction.

And do you not hold it to be the **highest commandment**: Love God above all and your neighbor as yourself? But who would want to love a God above all else, who

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s argument regarding the nature of God’s relationship to humanity. He transitions from discussing God’s justice and mercy to the practical implication of these attributes: the literal, organic connection between all people within the "body" of God.</meta>

...far and high above all is he who does not acknowledge the God who not only spreads His hands over all, but who carries everyone within everyone else in His deepest heart; who can never do harm in all eternity without suffering from it Himself; in whom you must seek everything you lack, from whom you must hope for everything you desire, and who—already here in the course of His justice which is only beginning for you, even in its very incompleteness—lets you glimpse what is destined one day for those who love Him with a righteous mind and act in the spirit of such love.

And who can love his neighbor better, or love him as a brother, than he who knows he is not cold and distant toward him? No—he is firmly grown together with him in the **communion** of the same highest Spirit, "one flesh" with him from the flesh of the same body, bound to him like a twin to a twin even before they leave the womb that carried them; for you have no more departed from the God who carries you <note>Fechner uses the analogy of a womb to describe our existence within God; just as a fetus is part of the mother, we are part of the divine.</note>.

And so, in everything, you profess in words exactly the same doctrine that I profess; you profess it, but you do not believe it, and you contradict yourself. Now, of course, a doctrine must appear strange to you that believes everything it professes, and which contradicts your own contradictions. But in doing so, it gains its very best quality.

While you speak of a God who is the refuge and source of all spirit, who <term>lives and moves and has His being<note>original: "lebt und webt und iſt"; a common German rendering of Acts 17:28, often used to emphasize God’s immanence in the world.</note></term> in you and you in Him—the <term>Knower of Hearts<note>original: "Herzenskündiger"; a traditional theological term for God's ability to see into the depths of human souls.</note></term>, the Uniter, the Infinite, the Omnipresent, the Omniscient, the Omnipotent, the All-loving, the All-good, the All-merciful, the All-just—you also wish again...

<summary>Fechner argues that if God is truly omnipresent and all-loving, then humans must be physically and spiritually interconnected as parts of God's own being. He suggests that neighborly love is not just a duty, but a recognition of our shared existence within the divine "body."</summary>

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s critique of the traditional, "external" view of God. On the previous page, he argued that while people profess God is everywhere, they act as if He is distant. Here, he explores the practical consequences of this distance, specifically regarding the efficacy of prayer and the immediate connection between the human and divine spirit.</meta>

...you position yourself externally toward Him, just as you position yourself toward your neighbor; and you position yourself toward your neighbor as if there were no bond between you in God—you on the right, he on the left, matter between you, God above, high in heaven, you on earth, and between heaven and earth, what a gap! Indeed, you finally lift God out beyond the entire world and banish from Him the evil one <note>Fechner refers here to the "Problem of Evil." He argues that traditional theology creates a contradiction by saying God created everything, but then placing "evil" outside of God’s domain.</note>, whom He first created; you deny everything you previously said, tear all the bonds you once recognized, and thereby destroy the greatest blessing of your faith. How far it is for you to where He dwells, and how near it is for me.

Let us contend for once as to whose prayer can be more successful: yours, you who position yourself with your thoughts *opposite* God, or mine, I who place myself with my thoughts *within* God Himself; that is where it will be revealed. But how many still believe in prayer today? That is where it already shows. Whether God hears it, whether He cares about it—who knows, who dares to believe it? And so it is soon abandoned entirely; fundamentally, it is seen as nothing more than an empty breath, vanishing with other breaths over the earth, which at most is His footstool <note>A reference to Isaiah 66:1: "Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool." Fechner is critiquing the idea that the physical world is merely a lowly object beneath God rather than part of Him.</note>. 

Is it the same with a thought that **lives and moves and has its being** <note>original: "lebt und webt und iſt"; a reference to Acts 17:28. Fechner uses this to describe the "panentheistic" view that we exist inside God like thoughts inside a mind.</note> in me, and I in it? Just as one of my thoughts, which exists entirely within me, can prompt me toward something, so I believe I can also seek to prompt God through a prayer—I, who with my prayer, exist entirely within God. Perhaps I follow my thought, perhaps I do not, depending on what seems good to me; just as God acts toward a praying soul. But this I know: that between the thought that seeks to prompt me and my own spirit, there is no gap that must first be traversed, which...

<summary>Fechner contrasts a distant, external God with his own view of God as an all-encompassing spirit. He argues that prayer is more effective when understood as a thought arising within the divine mind rather than a message sent to a distant location.</summary>

of prayer and the church community are not in vain.

<summary>Fechner argues that prayer is effective because human thoughts exist within God's mind, acting as internal impulses that God "hears" as immediately as we hear our own thoughts. He suggests that while prayer cannot "force" God's hand, intense and communal prayer increases the likelihood of a divine response, much like concentrated thoughts influence a human's decisions.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s discussion on the mechanics of prayer within a panpsychist framework. He addresses the potential paradox of "God praying to Himself" and uses a musical metaphor—the resolution of dissonance—to explain the presence of evil within a divine, all-encompassing spirit.</meta>

that is good; and He holds nothing good except that which is good, so I immediately ask for nothing that is not in the sense of the Good.

You say, O Folly: if I belong to God, then it is God who prays to Himself, who honors Himself, when I do it. But how, are you then God because you are *in* God? Do you not remain infinitely small compared to God? Is being the smallest moment and being the Whole the same thing? Should not even in me the small thought and the small desire give honor to my whole spirit, be hesitant to go against its sense, and turn back from time to time toward the whole spirit, considering what would most satisfy it, and stimulating it so that it may lead the thought further toward the goal?

Is it an evil thought that stimulates me? I punish it, I suppress it; yet I am not therefore evil myself, if I only punish it, only suppress it, and do not let it reach its ultimate goal. In this way, God punishes the evil spirit, which is His own part; but He is not the evil spirit, just as the symphony is not the dissonance <note>original: "Disharmonie"</note> of which it contains the resolution or the dissolution <note>Fechner uses the term "Aufhebung," a concept famously used by Hegel to mean both the canceling and the preservation of something at a higher level; here, it refers to musical resolution.</note>. This is an old image used to explain the existence of evil *with* God, but it only fits to explain the existence of evil *in* God, if it is to no longer be an evil for God Himself. For if the symphony allowed the dissonance to exist alongside it, but separate from it and unresolved within it, then and only then would it suffer through the accompanying and opposing discord <term>Mißklang: a jarring or unharmonious sound; a discordance</term>. And yet, this is how we mostly imagine evil in relation to God; the eternal discord of evil unresolved by God results in the eternal rejection of evil, results in eternal Hell.

<summary>Fechner argues that while human thoughts and even "evil spirits" exist within God, they do not make God evil, just as a symphony remains beautiful by resolving its dissonant notes. He critiques the traditional view of Hell as an eternal, unresolved discord outside of God's harmony.</summary>
<keywords>panpsychism, theodicy, dissonance, symphony metaphor, resolution, evil, prayer, divine harmony, Hell</keywords>

<meta>This page transitions from the metaphysical discussion of evil as a "dissonance" within God to the ethical consequences of this worldview. Fechner argues that because all individuals are parts of God, the commandment to love one's neighbor is a logical necessity of the "interconnectedness" (Zusammenhang) of the divine whole.</meta>

And can anyone act more effectively in the world according to the commandment of the love of God and neighbor <note>original: "Liebe Gottes und des Nächsten"</note> than one who knows that no divide exists between him and his neighbor—indeed, even the most distant person—within God and toward God; that whatever he does to any among them, he does to God? 

But God does not merely hold a single person within Himself; He holds all within Himself. Therefore, it is not just what you do for this or that specific person; no, whatever good you do in the world in general is done to God as a good act. So do not ask whether it is for you or for me, whether it is this or that, whether it is here or there, or whether it is today or tomorrow; ask instead: how is it best for the Whole, for the Eternal <note>original: "das Ganze, für das Ewige"</note>? For that is done only for God, the Whole and Eternal. 

Whether it is for you or for others, it is all one; you both belong to God, and there is no difference there. Thus, do it for yourself or do it for another, whichever is best for the Whole and for all the future. Do it according to commandments established in this spirit; those are the divine commandments.

But what do I call "good"? What is the meaning of the divine commandments? Were they given out of caprice? Are they intended to plague mankind? I recognize nothing in them but this meaning: that contentment <term>Genüge: A state of being "enough" or "sufficient," implying a deep sense of peaceful adequacy.</term> and satisfaction <note>original: "Befriedigung"</note> within the Whole, for everyone in their interconnectedness <term>Zusammenhang: A key term for Fechner, referring to the organic, conscious unity that links all individual experiences into the single experience of God.</term>, should be secured and grow as much as possible. It means that everyone should not simply have and do what they personally prefer at the expense of others, but that all should possess together and strive together for what can bring the greatest contentment and satisfaction to all of them collectively. And that is precisely what must most satisfy God, since He feels with all and through all, and above everything they feel individually, [He feels] the connection...

<summary>Fechner argues that ethical behavior is the logical result of panpsychism: since all people are parts of God, serving the "Whole" is the only way to truly serve God or oneself. He defines the "Good" as that which increases the collective contentment and satisfaction of all beings within the divine unity.</summary>

<keywords>ethics, love of neighbor, the Whole (das Ganze), divine commandments, interconnectedness (Zusammenhang), contentment (Genüge), panpsychism</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the ethical discussion from the previous page, moving from the definition of "good" as satisfaction within the interconnected whole to a specific critique of both pure egoism and extreme self-sacrifice. It establishes a "calculus of pleasure" where the individual's well-being is viewed as a constituent part of God's own joy.</meta>

...feels for the Whole. In this sense are the divine commandments. (See Vol. I, p. 379). <note>original: "Vgl. Th. I. S. 379." This refers to the first volume of the author's work.</note>

One person wants nothing but his own pleasure <term>Lust: In this context, "Lust" refers to a broad sense of joy, delight, or well-being, rather than just "lust" in the modern English sense.</term>; another says that merit lies only in sacrificing oneself for others. The one is as erroneous as the other. Whatever your pleasure takes away from the pleasure of the Whole <note>original: "Lust des Ganzen"</note>, in that you sin, if it happens with knowledge and with will; whatever you take away from your own pleasure, such that something is thereby lost to the total pleasure, in that you sin, if it happens with knowledge and will. 

For God wishes to harvest pleasure from your soul and your body just as much as from any other; how then should you manage the domain whose care He has primarily entrusted to you any worse than those over which He has placed others? Only beware of thinking that mere sensual pleasure <term>Sinnenlust: The gratification of the physical senses, which the author distinguishes from the higher or "total" pleasure of God.</term> is God’s pleasure; only beware of thinking that what you gain in pleasure here and now is also an immediate gain for the Whole, and thus for God; only beware of trying to calculate better with your weak insight than has long since been calculated across the Whole in the divine commandments. 

You are free only in what they leave free. They are the great brackets—not of individual pleasure <term>Einzellust</term>, but of the universal welfare <term>allgemeines Heil: This term carries a dual meaning of "general well-being" and "universal salvation."</term>, which carries all individual pleasures like small berries; for what, in the end, does the individual berry matter—whether this branch bears it or that one, whether this year bears it or that one; only trample nothing willfully; the care or the breaking of the shrub alone leads to blessing or to damnation. It is not a matter of sacrificing oneself for others, nor of sacrificing others to oneself, for those who wish to serve God; but—

<summary>This page argues that sin is any action that diminishes the total "pleasure" of the divine Whole, whether through selfish indulgence or unnecessary self-sacrifice. It positions the divine commandments as the necessary framework for maintaining the "shrub" of universal welfare, upon which all individual joys grow.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the sentence from page 10, completing the word "sondern" (but rather). It expands on the "calculus of pleasure" by distinguishing between fleeting individual desires and the "higher pleasure" that stems from the well-being of the whole.</meta>

...but rather be ready to sacrifice the small, brief pleasure, whether it be yours or mine, to the great, eternal, all-encompassing sources of pleasure, wherever a sacrifice is required; often, however, it is also simply a matter of drawing from them; and that which is sacrificed only breaks forth as a richer blessing in another place; otherwise, it would be no true sacrifice; for God wishes to lose nothing, but often to gain through deferral <note>original: "Verschieben". This suggests a temporary postponement of gratification for a greater eventual gain across time or space.</note>.

Above all lower pleasure, there is a higher pleasure, a pleasure above pleasure, a joy above joy, which hovers like the dove over the green crops—that is, the pleasure, the joy, the delight in that which is itself pleasure-giving and joy-giving; and this pleasure, this joy, this delight becomes all the greater and higher, the larger the context and the further out I feel or recognize the security and conditions of that pleasure and joy; and the righteous person does not separate their own pleasure from the pleasure of others. God will also have this higher joy in me if I direct my striving so that, in the broadest context and for the longest duration, it serves not the [fleeting] desires but the sources of pleasure in the world, in the sense of promoting happiness, salvation <term>Heil: In German, this encompasses both religious salvation and general well-being or "wholeness."</term>, and blessing. And I will have this higher joy in God because I know that He cannot direct His striving in any way other than toward the ultimate and greatest possible satisfaction <term>Genügen: A state of sufficiency or fulfillment where the needs of the soul are met.</term> for me and for all; since His own satisfaction is not separate from that of His creatures; and if everything is not now as I would like it to be, I know that God Himself suffers with me, in the lower realms of His being <term>Wesen: The nature, essence, or fundamental existence of a being.</term>, and possesses in His higher power and His higher knowledge the means to [unite] me with Himself—

<meta>This page completes the sentence from page 11 regarding "satisfaction" (Genügen). It transitions into a philosophical defense of panentheism—the idea that the world and humanity exist within God rather than being external to Him. The author uses the psychological analogy of "representations" in the mind to explain how something can be both "inside" a spirit and yet "opposite" to it.</meta>

...to satisfy at the same time; but that he knows he can do it, and I know he can do it, gives both him and me the highest satisfaction <term>Genügen: A state of fulfillment or being "enough."</term>.

How differently everything appears if I must imagine myself as being externally opposite to God, and must imagine a spiritually empty space between me and my fellow human being. Does not everything then become distant which here is immediate, everything fall apart which here is bound into one, everything become incomprehensible which here is self-evident; everything a dead decree <note>original: "Satzung"; implies a formal, imposed rule.</note> which here is a living drive?

Truly, I would not sell for any small price the faith that I am **in** God, not **opposite** to God. And yet, yes, I am opposite to God—we all are—but only internally, not externally opposite. Confusing these two is the error that we, of course, constantly commit. For we also place thoughts and perceptions "opposite" to ourselves; we call them "representations" <term>Vorstellungen: In German philosophy, this refers to the mental images or ideas "placed before" (vor-stellen) the mind for examination.</term>; yet they remain no less within us because of it. In fact, the more vividly we place them before us, the more they belong to us, the more actively our spirit proves itself within them, and the more actively they prove themselves within our spirit. Being "opposite" to a higher Spirit is not like being "opposite" to another physical body. Of course, it would be just as erroneous if we thought we stood opposite to God in no different way than our spirit stands to its own mental representations; we stand opposite to God with unspeakably more independence, self-power, and self-consciousness than our representations stand to us; as we have said so often before, but only because God's Spirit is even more unspeakably independent, self-powerful, self-con— <note>The word "selbstbewusst" (self-conscious) is cut off and continues on the next page.</note>

The presence of the ruling God is expressed more frequently, more beautifully, and with the mark of a deeper conviction by Rückert than is usual—where it is often found merely in poetic flowery language <note>original: "Verblümung" – meaning to speak in metaphors or to "sugarcoat" a truth with ornamental imagery.</note>. > When the sublime amazes young humanity,
> It speaks in a bright dream: "A god has done this."
> And when it then awakens to the feeling of the beautiful,
> It confesses with joyful pride: "Man has accomplished it."
> And when one day it ripens to the Truth, it will recognize:
> It is God doing it within man, who is not to be separated from Him.
(Vol. I. p. 9).

---

> Worthy of human speech is not what men have done;
> With Nature and with God my spirit shall consult.
> The wisdom of India has forgotten history,
> So that it may report only of God, Nature, and Spirit.

> Done, or seen done—forgotten it with God in God,
> And now know only one thing more, and know this one thing fully:
> God is the Sun of Spirits <term>Geistersonn': A metaphor representing God as the central source of light, life, and warmth for all individual souls.</term> and Nature is His radiance.
(Vol. I. p. 39).

> Selfhood is so narrow, divinity so wide.
> Be yourself! He Himself wills that you should be yourself,
> So that you yourself may recognize that He alone is your Self.
> Remember this! You have only forgotten it;
> Let yourself be reminded! He reminds you of it constantly.

Just as many rays go from the sun toward the earth,
So a ray goes from God into the heart of every thing.
By this ray, the thing is connected to God,

### 9. I have it from God, and God from me.
That God is so blessed, and lives without desire,
He has received as well from me, as I from him. <note>Silesius suggests a mutual dependency where God's "bliss" is only realized through his relationship with the human soul.</note>

### 10. I am like God, and God like me.
I am as great as God, he is as small as I;
He cannot be above me, nor I beneath him. <note>This reflects the mystical concept of "Gleichheit" or "likeness," where in the state of divine union, distinctions of scale and rank vanish.</note>

### 18. I do as God does.
God loves me more than himself; if I love him more than myself:
Then I give him as much as he gives me from within himself.

### 68. Deep calls to deep. <note>original: "Ein Abgrund ruft den andern." A reference to Psalm 42:7, repurposed here for mystical thought.</note>
The abyss of my spirit calls always with a cry
Upon the abyss of God: say, which may be deeper. <term>Abyss: In German mysticism (Abgrund), this refers to the bottomless, unknowable nature of the divine and the human soul.</term>

### 73. Man was God’s life.
Before I even became something, I was God’s life:
Therefore he has also given himself entirely for me.

### 79. God bears perfect fruit.
Whoever would deny me perfection, such as God has,
Would first have to break me from his vine. <note>An allusion to the New Testament metaphor (John 15) of the vine and the branches, implying that the believer is an organic part of God.</note>

### 88. Everything lies within man.
How can you, O man, still long for anything more,
Since you hold God and all things embraced within yourself?

### 90. The Godhead is the green.
The Godhead is my sap! What greens and blooms from me,
That is his Holy Spirit, through whom the vital impulse happens.

### 96. God can do nothing without me.
God cannot make a single little worm without me:
If I do not sustain it with him, it must straightway fall to pieces. <note>original: "stracks zu krachen," literally "straightway to a crash."</note>

### 100. One holds the other.
God is as much concerned with me as I am with him,
I help him preserve his essence, as he tends to mine.

### 105. God’s Image.
->I bear God’s image: if He wishes to look upon Himself,<-
->It can only happen in me, and in those who are like me.<- <note>Silesius suggests that God is a "hidden" God who only achieves self-consciousness or visibility by reflecting Himself in the mirror of the human soul.</note>

### 106. The One in the Other.
->I am not outside of God, and God is not outside of me,<-
->I am His radiance and light, and He is my adornment.<-

### 115. You Yourself Must Be the Sun.
->I myself must be the sun; I must, with my rays,<-
->Paint the colorless sea of the entire Godhead.<- <note>The "colorless sea" is a common mystical metaphor for the absolute, undifferentiated essence of God—the "Divine Dark" that requires the human spirit to give it "color" or form.</note>

### 121. Through Humanity to the Godhead.
->If you wish to catch the pearl-dew of the noble Godhead,<-
->Then you must hang unswervingly upon His humanity.<- <note>This refers to the Christological bridge; one reaches the abstract "Godhead" through the lived reality of Christ's "humanity."</note>

### 129. Evil Arises from You.
->God is indeed nothing but good: condemnation, death, and pain,<-
->And what one calls evil, must, O Man, exist only in you.<-

### 136. How God Rests in Me.
->You must be completely pure, and stand in a <term>Now</term>,<-
->If God is to see Himself in you, and rest more gently.<- <term>The "Now" (German: Nun): In mystical tradition, this refers to the *nunc stans* or the "Eternal Now," a state of being where time ceases to exist and one is fully present with the Divine.</term>

### 200. God is Nothing (Created).
->God is truly nothing: and if He is something,<-
->It is only in me, as He chooses me for Himself.<- <note>Here, "nothing" does not mean non-existence, but rather "no-thing." God is not a "thing" or an object among other objects in the created world.</note>

### 204. Man is the Highest Thing.
->Nothing seems high to me: I am the highest thing,<-
->Because even God without me is small to Himself.<- <note>This is one of Silesius's most radical statements of reciprocity, suggesting that God’s greatness is only realized through His relationship with His creation.</note>

### 237. One Prays Rightly in the Interior.
->Man, if you wish to know what it means to pray honestly,<-
->Then go within yourself, and ask God’s Spirit.<-

### 238. Essential Prayer.
->He who lives with a pure heart, and walks on Christ’s path,<-
->He prays essentially to God within himself.<- <note>To pray "essentially" means to pray with one's very being (Wesen) rather than merely with words.</note>

> “In the poetic descriptions of nature, it is shown how the Indian poet views nature with entirely different eyes than we are accustomed to from our religious standpoint. Above all, it is always a **religious reverence** by which he is seized when contemplating nature. Its grandeur, its brilliance, its richness overwhelms him, and thereby the description—though it occurs only occasionally and belongs to the external scenery—momentarily acquires an independent significance. Furthermore, however, natural forms are most intimately related to man himself for the Indian poet. Like man, they are manifestations of the **One divine life**. It is therefore not merely a poetic license when the entire natural environment of man is depicted as sentient, when man calls upon nature for sympathy, when he questions it, when he communicates his joy and his sorrow to it.” (Schaller, *Letters* p. 54). <note>Julius Schaller (1810–1868) was a German philosopher; here the author quotes his "Letters on Alexander von Humboldt's Kosmos" to illustrate how ancient Indian literature viewed nature as a living, divine entity.</note>

“So be it,” you say, “that we are **members of God**; but if we are members of God, why be members of the Earth? Is it not enough to think of ourselves as members of God?”

And indeed, it would suffice if it were only a matter of idle thinking. But if, instead of fruitlessly spinning the distaff of contemplation around itself, we spin out the thread of thought from the actual state of things, we find that it proceeds in a natural sequence from our own individual <term>soul-animation<gloss>Beseelung: the state of being endowed with a soul or living spirit</gloss></term> to a **universal soul-animation**, just as, looking backward, it moves only through the intermediate link of an individual soul-animation of the **stars**. Everything written in this book is but the movement of the finger that glided up and down from the distaff to the spool in this direction. <note>The author uses a textile metaphor—the distaff and the spool—to describe how a logical argument is "spun" from observations of the world.</note>

Moreover, this intermediate level, which has been constructed between God and us through intellectual means, is not fruitless for the satisfaction of higher and warmer needs. For on the one hand, God is thereby raised by one degree in our conception; on the other hand, we simultaneously step one degree closer to Him. Previously, God seemed too close in His greatness and yet too far in His distance, as we applied only the highest human yardstick to Him, while simultaneously pushing Him beyond all human horizons. 

But now He appears to us as a being not only beyond our own reason and senses, but also beyond the reason and senses of beings that are themselves already highly superhuman. <note>The author refers to the Earth and stars as "superhuman beings" possessing their own consciousness, acting as a bridge between the individual human and the infinite God.</note> Once, God stood as a tower stands beside a man; there was nothing between us and God but misty figures, and we measured the tower of God by the smallness of man. ## XIII. Christian Matters.

<margin>\* 1 Corinthians 3:11.</margin>
> For no one can lay any foundation
> other than the one already laid, which
> is Jesus Christ \*.

The Christian may well ask: what do you have to do with Christianity? Are these not entirely new things? Did Christ ever even speak of such matters?

I ask in return: did He ever contradict them? And is anything written here in contradiction to what Christ has spoken?

But where was Christ Himself spoken of? Should we not now seek everything differently that we previously sought in Him and found through Him? Should we no longer regard Him as the <term>Mediator|Mittler; a figure who bridges the gap between the divine and the human</term>, <term>Healer-Prophet|Heilkünder; one who announces or teaches the way to spiritual healing and salvation</term>, and <term>Savior|Heilbringer; literally "the bringer of salvation or healing"</term>?

And if He has not been spoken of until now, let it be so now. Despite everything, I say: I remain a Christian. I do not intend to dissolve His <term>Covenant|Bund; the sacred bond or agreement between God and humanity</term>; no, rather to strengthen it and to entwine myself further within it—that is the purpose of the work being woven here.

The book <note>Likely referring to the Bible or the New Testament.</note> that speaks of Him, through which He speaks, and has spoken through all the time following Him, has spoken...

...the Almighty, the All-Good, the All-Loving, the All-Just, and the All-Merciful. Once I came to a city full of houses and palaces made of brick, hewn stone, and marble, all built purposefully and with regularity, firmly joined together and each vying with the next in ornamentation. Yet in the center stood an old hut, awkward, useful for no human purpose, full of hatches, holes, and dark corners; nothing fit together; it lacked clamps, struts, and supports; it was a miracle that it still held together. And I laughed at the hut, this remnant of an old, half-barbaric age in such a beautiful, rich city, and I said: tomorrow it will be rubble. And when I returned after a hundred years, all the houses and palaces around it were rubble—rubble or rebuilt—and others stood nearby in different places, according to new rules and for new purposes. The old hut, however, stood in the middle in its old place, unchanged, with its hatches, holes, and dark corners, the same as if I were seeing it the day before a hundred years ago, as if the tooth of time <note>original: "Zahn der Zeit"; a common idiom referring to the slow decay caused by the passage of time</note>, which breaks everything, had been broken upon it. And again after a hundred, and yet another hundred years, it was always thus: the old hut was still the same, while everything around it was new. Then I said: "Thus God's power sustains it." And from the houses and palaces came many a sick and many a weary person, languishing in the streets and unable to recover, and no doctor could help; yet whoever entered the hut, which itself seemed in need of a doctor, became healthy and joyful. Then I said: "Here dwells God’s salvation <term>salvation<gloss>Heil; in German, this word carries the dual meaning of 'salvation' and 'healing' or 'wholeness'</gloss></term>."

The old hut—unsuitable for human purposes, poorly joined according to human rules, with its hatches, holes, dark corners, and missing clamps, struts, and supports—that is the <term>Holy Scripture<gloss>The Bible, which the author portrays here as a humble but divinely protected structure.</gloss></term>. But how was it possible that the Bible—if it is God’s work and word, even if brought to us through human hands—carries so many flaws on every side? First ask, then, how was it possible that the world—which is also God’s work, also created through God’s word—carries so many flaws on every side? If the one is possible, so is the other. The Bible, of course, is meant to be a divine or God-inspired <term>gottbegeistet: literally "God-spirited"; the idea that the text is animated by a divine breath rather than being a cold record</term> work in a different sense than other works in the world. It reflects to you, along with God, his world of imperfections; yet in such a way that God shines through it all the more for those who seek him therein, just as the imperfections appear all the more to those who seek *them*. ## The Kingdoms of Heaven and the Hereafter

With the first aspect of this doctrinal concept <note>German: *Lehrbegriffs*. This refers to the systematic framework of religious or philosophical belief Fechner is constructing.</note> we concern ourselves particularly here; with the second, in the following part of this work, which deals with "future things" <note>This refers to Eschatology, the study of the end of life and the world.</note>. Christianity, however, does not consist merely of a theoretical doctrine regarding the kingdom of heaven and the hereafter—one that has been passed down from Christ to those who profess faith in him—but also of a **real mediation** of the highest spiritual blessings <note>German: *Heilsgüter*; literally "goods of salvation." These are the spiritual benefits or "treasures" promised to the believer.</note> of the kingdom of heaven and the hereafter for them through his person. Thus, faith in the mediation <term>Mediation (Vermittelung)</term><note>In this context, mediation refers to the act of Christ serving as the bridge or "go-between" for humanity and God.</note> through his person itself belongs to this very process of mediation. Even the recognition of this mediation, which once seemed to contradict **reason**, will find its foundation within our teaching.

Let us look back once more. A heavenly being <note>Fechner likely refers here to the "Earth-Spirit" or the soul of the Earth, a central idea in his philosophy where the planet itself is a conscious, divine entity.</note> takes over the mediation between God and us in every possible relationship concerning the earthly realm as a whole. This being is the steward of all our earthly affairs—from the most material to the most spiritual, from the lowest to the highest, without any distinction. It is mother, nurse, and so much more for us. 

However, even regarding its own highest concerns, this being desires to be mediated with God in such a way that everything lower and subordinate may receive direction, fruit, and salvation from it. It can find this mediator only in the highest thing at its disposal: in the (this-worldly and other-worldly) **human**. Thus, that heavenly being as a whole not only cannot replace a human mediator for us, but can only find that mediator within humanity, in a son—

### Bethlehem and Golgatha

He was born in Bethlehem,
He who has brought us life,
And Golgatha he chose,
To break the power of death through the cross.
I traveled from the evening shore <note>The "evening shore" refers to the West or Europe.</note>

How the host of earthly strength
Has succumbed before the power of heaven!
I saw them, wherever I might wander,
Fallen into their ruins,
While standing in silent glory
Are only Bethlehem and Golgatha.

Away with you, Egyptian pyramids!
In which man took such pains to build
Only the darkness of the grave,
Not the peace of death.
You Sphinxes of colossal size,
You could not solve for the earth
The riddle of life, as it was solved
Through Bethlehem and Golgatha.

But a knot that links spirits together is itself a spirit. That is the **Earth Spirit**. Now, through Christ, this knot has been drawn together even more tightly and intimately, so that it has become a knot in a higher sense than it was before. And does it contradict Christ’s teaching if we also link the souls of all the stars in God, just as Christ links the souls of all humanity? The difference is that Christ did this for humanity not merely externally in words—as we do and can only do regarding the stars—but in deed, in substance, and in life; he did not merely point out the connection, but formed it himself in the highest and best sense, which is, of course, something else entirely. <note>Fechner argues that while we can only philosophize about the "souls" of stars, Christ actually embodied and created the spiritual unity of humanity.</note>

**Christ** is the living eye that surveys all the herds of the earth as one, pasturing them and making them flourish.

That the view of a **soul-endowment** <term>Beseelung: the animation of matter by a soul</term> of the stars does not contradict the original foundations of Christianity can be proven *a posteriori* <term>a posteriori: reasoning based on observed facts or historical evidence</term> by the fact that in the earliest times of Christianity, no heresy was found in that view, as the Bible itself does not speak clearly on the matter. Some, specifically the Church Father **Origen**, even declared themselves directly in favor of this belief. Later, of course, the negative view prevailed. The author uses this quote to show that while later theologians like Petavius dismissed the idea as "old-wives' tales," it was once part of serious Christian thought.</note>

...infected their minds; these views are read more extensively in the first book of *On First Principles* <term>De Principiis: Origen’s foundational work on Christian theology</term>, in chapter seven, and are inserted in passing in the *Commentaries on the Gospel of John*: where he suspects that Christ even suffered for the stars themselves. <note>original: "ubi pro astris ipsis suspicatur passum esse Christum." "Those things which are in heaven, the stars, are **animated beings** <term>astra animata: stars possessing their own souls</term> endowed with reason, and are illuminated by the light of knowledge by Wisdom, who is the splendor of eternal light. For their physical light is the work of the universal Creator: but their spiritual light is perhaps also their own, perfected by their free will."

"Furthermore, the one who published the *Apology for Origen* under the name of Pamphilus <note>Pamphilus of Caesarea was a scholar whose defense of Origen was later translated and likely edited by the monk Rufinus.</note> (which was interpolated by Rufinus, and which we discuss elsewhere), says that there are various opinions in the Churches concerning the **heavenly lights**: some think they are living beings endowed with reason; others think they do not even have sensation: yet neither group is judged as heretics by the others. Thus Origen himself in the Preface to the books *On First Principles*: 'Concerning the Sun,' he says, 'and Moon and Stars, whether they are living beings or inanimate, is not clearly handed down.'"

"Besides Origen, the pseudo-Clement <note>The "Clementine Recognitions" are an early Christian philosophical novel once attributed to Clement of Rome.</note> in the fifth book of the *Recognitions* holds the same opinion. In that work, Peter, speaking against the worshippers of idols, speaks thus:

'Do you then worship something that cannot feel, when every person with senses would not even believe that those things made by God which *do* have senses ought to be worshipped? That is, the Sun and the Moon, or the stars, and all things that are in heaven and on earth. For they think it just to venerate not those things made for the service of the world, but the Creator of those things and of the whole world. For even these stars rejoice when He is worshipped and honored: and they are unwilling for the honor of the Creator to be deferred to the creature.'

Ambrose also seems to hold a similar opinion, as do Jerome and Augustine. For Augustine clearly confessed to others that he was in doubt, even though in other places he taught no less clearly that those celestial bodies lack sensation."

# XIV. Concluding Reflections, Historical Notes.

Let us return, in conclusion, with several reflections back to those of the introduction.

While the idea that the celestial bodies <term>Gestirne: A term encompassing stars, planets, and other heavenly bodies</term> are higher beings endowed with souls no longer seems to fit—or wishes to fit—into any of our scientific or religious systems, it is, by contrast, the most natural expression of the earliest, most unbiased way of observing nature: the first revelation of the Divine to humanity. All peoples whom we can still observe in their infancy—indeed, many into their most beautiful youth, and some even after many thousands of years of development—seek the Divine *within* rather than *outside* or *above* nature; they give God a body to accompany the spirit, and do not separate the two outside of themselves, just as they do not know how to separate them within themselves. The worship of God <term>Gottesdienst</term> is a worship of nature <term>Naturdienst</term>. Within this worship of nature, however, the veneration of the stars—as the most noble individualizations of the Divine—occupies the highest place. Indeed, one can assert that among all natural objects, none have been more frequently, steadfastly, or highly revered than the celestial bodies, above all the Sun and Moon. Peoples who otherwise have almost nothing in common with one another, <note>The author is likely referring to the universal nature of solar and lunar myths across disparate cultures like the Egyptians, Aztecs, and Indo-Europeans.</note>

<summary>This chapter opening reflects on the historical shift from ancient "nature-worship," where stars were seen as divine living beings, to modern systems that separate the physical universe from the spiritual. Greeks, Persians, Hindus, Greenlanders, Nadowessians <note>A historical name for the Sioux or Dakota people of North America.</note> etc., etc., agree in this belief—the best proof that they did not borrow it from one another, but rather drew it from a common source of nature <term>Naturquell</term>.

The belief in the divinity of the celestial bodies <term>Gestirne: A term encompassing stars, planets, and other heavenly bodies</term> is, in fact, different from the particularities that characterize the faiths of the Jews <term>Judenthum</term>, Muslims <term>Mohammedaner</term>, and—let us add—the Christians <term>Christenthum</term> themselves, in contrast to one another. These particularities are believed by people only to the extent that they have learned about them from other people; and if all Jews, Muslims, and Christians were to die out at once, and the Koran and the Bible were destroyed, then it would be over forever for Judaism, Islam <term>Islam</term>, and Christianity in the specific sense in which they now confront one another. This is true even though the general and eternal truths—which Christianity partly shares with other religions <term>Religion</term> and partly possesses beyond them—would necessarily assert themselves anew; yet they would assert themselves no more surely than the veneration of the celestial bodies. 

Even if all star-worshipers <term>Gestirnanbeter</term> were to die, this worship would always begin anew if humanity were to begin anew, because the prompting causes for it are found inherently and innately within the nature of things and within humans themselves.

Wherein do these promptings lie? In the brilliance, the splendor, the height, the unreachability, the independent course, the mysterious order of the stars, and the dependence of man and all of nature upon them in the most pervasive and universal relationships.

If there were no such natural prompts, if only a mere appearance of them had been produced at a specific time and place, only then might one speak of a deception. But such prompts truly exist. Even the **instinct** of animals is correctly guided by natural causes which we simply do not understand in the same way as the animals do. ...to the creator. Therefore, among the Hindus, the sun god is simultaneously the demiurge <note>A term from Greek philosophy, here meaning a secondary creator or artisan-like deity responsible for fashioning the physical world.</note>. In Peru, the sun god is likewise the creator. That supreme god of the Siberian peoples dwells not only in the heavens or in the sun; rather, the sun itself is considered to be this spirit (Stuhr, *Religions of the East*, p. 244), and during the great spring festival, the descent of the sun god is celebrated (Görres, *History of Asian Myths*, 55).... The Indigenous peoples themselves perceive their Great Spirit as a sun god. This is evident from several names: *Harakouannentakton* <note>A Mohawk name</note> refers to the one who "binds the sun," while the Huron deity *Areskowi* and the Iroquois deity *Agriskove* are both sun gods. 

However, others distinguish between the sun god and the Great Spirit. Among the Delaware <note>The Lenape people</note>, the god of the heavens is the supreme god, while the sun is the second (Loskiel <note>George Henry Loskiel, a Moravian missionary and historian</note>). Indeed, the Chippewa <note>The Ojibwe people</note> branch of the Lenape <note>Fechner groups various Algonquian-speaking tribes under the broader "Lenape" umbrella here, reflecting 19th-century ethnographic views</note> worships the Great Spirit *Manedo* <note>Manitou</note>, but neither the sun nor the moon. While the Great Spirit may be less identified with the sun god among some Lenni Lenape, the Florida peoples—the Apalachee, the Natchez, and others—certainly form a significant exception. 

Yet even among other Lenni Lenape groups, such as the Creeks, the Great Spirit was worshipped as the sun. In other Lenape traditions, during the great festival of *Kitschi Manitu* <note>Gitchi Manitou, the Great Spirit</note>, peace pipes are lit in honor of the sun, and at sunrise, the women offer their children to the sun. However, we find the Great Spirit worshipped as a sun god even more generally among the Mingo <note>Iroquoian-speaking</note> tribes. The "Lord of Life" or "The Old Man Who Never Dies," as they frequently call the Great Spirit, is either the sun itself—as seen with the Mandan, Hidatsa <note>Original: *Mönitarris*</note>, and Blackfoot tribes—or, which amounts to the same thing, the Lord of Life has his seat within the sun. The Sioux <note>Original: *Nadowessier*</note> also consider the sun to be the creator; they sacrifice the best of their hunt to it, offer the first smoke of their pipes, and pray to it at sunrise.....

Just as the supreme and universal god in Siberia is often simultaneously the heavens and the sun (Stuhr, p. 244), the Iroquois Great Spirit *Agriskove* and the Huron *Areskowi* likewise unite both concepts of sky and sun within themselves. In other instances, however, the Great Spirit is frequently worshipped solely as a god of the heavens.

<meta>Following the previous page's discussion on sun worship among Indigenous American and Asian cultures, this page transitions to Western intellectual history, examining how ancient Greek and Roman philosophers viewed the stars and nature as divine, living entities.</meta>

How common the view of an ensoulment of nature <note>The idea that nature possesses a soul or consciousness, often called panpsychism.</note> in general, and in connection with this, the stars in particular, was to the ancient philosophers—who based their views more on the observation of nature and a natural perception of things than those of today—may be taught by the following passages from Cicero's *On the Nature of the Gods* <note>Latin: *De natura deorum*</note>.

> Book I, chapter 11. Alcmaeon of Croton <term>Crotoniates</term> attributed divinity to the sun, the moon, and the rest of the stars, and furthermore to the soul.... Pythagoras held that there is a soul extending and moving through the entire nature of things, from which our own souls are plucked.... Xenophanes, by adding a mind, willed that everything infinite should be God.... Parmenides calls the continuous heat of the light-filled sphere, which encircles the sky, God.....

> Ch. 12. The same writer (Plato) says both in the *Timaeus* and in the *Laws* that the world is God, as are the sky, the stars, the earth, the souls, and those deities whom we have accepted from the traditions of our ancestors.

> Ch. 13. Aristotle at one time attributes all divinity to the mind; at another time he says the world itself is God; at another he places someone else over the world and assigns him the role of ruling and maintaining the movement of the world through a kind of revolution; then he says the heat of the sky is God.

> Ch. 14. Xenocrates says there are eight gods: five who are named among the wandering stars <note>The five planets known in antiquity</note>; one who should be considered a single God composed of all the stars fixed in the sky, as if from scattered limbs; he adds the sun as the seventh and the moon as the eighth. From the same school of Plato, Heraclides of Pontus <term>Heraclides Ponticus</term> filled his books with childish fables: at one time he thinks the world is divine, then the mind; he also attributes divinity to the wandering stars, yet strips God of sensation and wishes his form to be changeable; and in the same book, he again refers to the earth and the sky as gods. Nor indeed is the inconsistency of Theophrastus to be endured. For at one time he attributes divine sovereignty to the mind, at another to the sky, and then to the signs and celestial stars. Nor should his student Strato be listened to, he who is called the Physicist <term>Physicus</term>.

Book II. Ch. 11. (Balbus the Stoic:) It is nature, therefore, which contains the whole world and protects it, and she does so not without sensation and reason. For every nature that is not solitary or simple, but joined and connected with another, must necessarily have some governing principle within itself—as the mind is in man, and in the beast something similar to the mind, from which the appetites for things arise.... Moreover, we see that in the parts of the world (for there is nothing in the whole world that is not a part of the universe) sensation and reason are present. In that part, therefore, in which the governing principle of the world resides, these things must necessarily be present, and indeed more sharply and greatly. Wherefore it is necessary that the world be wise, and that the nature which holds all things embraced should excel in the perfection of reason, and therefore that the world is God, and all the power of the world is contained by divine nature.

<meta>Continuing from the previous page, the text persists with excerpts from Book II of Cicero’s *On the Nature of the Gods*. Having established that the universe is governed by a rational force, the speaker Balbus—representing the Stoic school of thought—now argues that the world itself, and the celestial bodies within it, must be living, intelligent, divine beings due to the presence of "vital heat."</meta>

...moved of its own accord, rather than by an external force. <note>original: *sponte moveatur, quam quod pulsu agitetur alieno*</note> He places this motion in the soul alone, and believes that the beginning of motion is derived from souls. Therefore, since all motion arises from the heat of the world, and that heat is not moved by an external impulse but by its own accord, it must necessarily be a soul. From this, it follows that the world is a living being. And from this also it can be understood that intelligence resides in it, because the world is certainly better than any other nature. For just as there is no part of our body that is not of less value than we ourselves are, so the whole universe must be of more value than any part of the universe. If this is so, it is necessary that the world is wise. For if it were not so, man—who is a part of the world and a sharer in reason—would have to be of more value than the whole world.

Ch. 15. (*Balbus the Stoic:*) And having perceived this divinity of the world, the same divinity must be attributed to the stars. These are born from the most mobile and purest part of the ether; they have no other nature mixed into them, but are entirely hot and transparent. Thus, they too may most rightly be described as living beings that feel and understand...

Therefore, since the fire of the sun is similar to those fires which are in the bodies of living beings, the sun also must be a living being, as must the other stars which arise in the celestial heat, which is named ether or heaven. Since the birth of some living beings occurs on land, others in water, and others in the air, it seemed absurd to Aristotle to think that no living animal is generated in that part which is most fit for creating animals. <note>Aristotle argued that each element—earth, water, air—had its inhabitants, so the "fire" of the heavens (ether) must also have inhabitants: the stars.</note> The stars occupy the ethereal region; since this region is very thin, always in motion, and vigorous, it is necessary that any animal born in it possesses the sharpest senses and the swiftest mobility. Therefore, since the stars are born in the ether, it is consistent that sense and intelligence are within them. From which it follows that the stars must be counted among the number of the Gods.

The learned Alexandrian Jew, Philo, also recognizes the divine spiritual nature of the stars, saying of them:

"For these are said to be living beings, and moreover, rational living beings..." <note>original Greek: Οὗτοι γὰρ ζῷά τε εἶναι λέγονται, καὶ ζῷα νοερά, μᾶλλον. Philo of Alexandria was a philosopher who sought to harmonize Jewish scripture with Greek philosophy.</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "primal state" of human understanding. knowledge <term>Erkenntniß</term> <note>While often translated as "knowledge," in this philosophical context, it refers to a deep, intuitive cognition or realization.</note>, which in another way is born within that of the most imperfect knowledge. He possesses the whole truth, but only in its entirely raw form, and without the slightest clarity regarding the individual moments <note>The author uses "moments" in the philosophical sense to mean specific stages, aspects, or constituent parts of a larger whole.</note> of this truth; he is wiser than the wisest among us and more childish than the most childish of our schoolchildren. In this course of development <term>Entwickelungsgang</term>, he now errs a thousandfold; he falls away from that state which was, in certain respects, most perfect. His knowledge, which was at first given to him as a whole, becomes piecemeal <term>Stückwerk</term> <note>Literally "piece-work," referencing the biblical idea (1 Corinthians 13:9) of knowing only in part or fragments.</note>, because he takes the parts or pieces for the whole, or misjudges their correct relationship to the whole—which he no longer oversees because he occupies himself too much with this or that individual thing, or confuses a distinction in observation with a division in the subject matter itself. But precisely through this, he learns to know the individual aspects and pieces in their particular relations to one another better and better; and as the knowledge of these individual relations constantly expands, and all advancements in science <note>The German *Wissenschaft* implies a systematic body of knowledge, including philosophy and theology, not just the hard sciences.</note> take their place, they naturally reconnect with one another. Contradictions cancel each other out, harmonies endure, and thus there is a constant urge toward a reunion in unity.

<meta>This page completes the thought from the previous page regarding how man loses sight of the whole by focusing on fragments. It describes the final stage of intellectual development: the return to a conscious unity.</meta>

...and truth, which for the first state of knowledge <term>Erkenntniß</term> <note>In this philosophical context, "Erkenntniß" refers to a deep, intuitive cognition or realization rather than just factual information.</note> had not yet been dissolved at all. In this way, man finally regains the full, unifying overview <term>Ueberschauung</term> of the whole; but now with a sharp gaze that correctly separates and connects every individual detail within it. Between the beginning and the end lies the richness and fullness of development <term>Entwickelung</term>, but also wrong paths and conflict.

In a certain sense, it is with truth just as it is with a work of art <term>Kunstwerk</term>, which is first presented to man complete and beautiful, then taken apart and thus destroyed by him in order to become knowledgeable about the inner workings of the individual parts, and finally reassembled into the full whole, where it only then achieves its full effect and meaning; now he sees it again in the same form as the unrefined eye once saw it; only now, deep insight has been added to that unrefined gaze. In the intervening time, much lack of clarity and discord <term>Zerwürfniß</term> arises; indeed, the memory of the whole and the knowledge of how it fits together is often completely lost, until—once the meaning of every individual part is correctly recognized—it naturally presses toward being joined together again.

Paganism <note>original: "Heidenthum." But a single seed lay for a long time, inconspicuous beneath them, enclosed within its own small roundness, believing itself to be the whole world <note>original: "das ganze Rund." A play on words between the roundness of the seed and the "round" of the globe.</note>. Yet a tiny germ slept within it—this germ is Christ, embedded there by a higher hand. 

When the time had come, it awakened and broke the seed, which then fell away. The grain emerged, at first small and much oppressed by the herbs and weeds all around it. Yet it grew ever higher as a straight trunk; it became stronger and stronger, driving roots out in every direction and drawing in saps and vital forces. The herbs and weeds around it died away, and their blossoms died with them. The trunk continued to rise straight upward, as if its only goal were to break free from the earth. Finally, it rooted through the entire earth like a single clod of soil, so that everything within became interconnected; what was loose became whole. Where there had been dry soil, life-fluids now flowed deep in the stillness. 

But the surface above began to grow desolate because of this single trunk, which climbed upward rich in leaves but poor in blossoms—save for one rank side-shoot <note>original: "geiler Seitenschoß." In 19th-century botany, "geil" refers to luxuriant, over-abundant growth that is often sterile or lacks flowers, here perhaps suggesting the worldly or institutional power of the Church.</note> near the ground, which, though a weed itself, helped to displace other weeds. At last, the tree itself seems weary of fruitlessly bringing forth ever more new branches; within it, things function only mechanically and predictably—until one day, in a new springtime <note>original: "Lenze," a poetic German term for spring.</note>, from the summit of the trunk, a crown of blossoms...

# XV. Appendix to the third section.

## A. Additions concerning the aesthetic judgment of the form and color of the Earth.

->(Compare Vol. I, p. 86 ff.)<-

**Undisputedly**, it has been proposed more than once, and not without reason, that the <term>spherical form<note>original: "Kugelgestalt." In Fechner’s philosophy, the sphere is not just a geometric shape but a symbol of divine perfection and self-containment.</note></term> is the most perfect form; however, it cannot be the most perfect for the formation of man, because man, as a human being, is still a very subordinate creature, and every form can only be called perfect in its kind to the degree that it corresponds to the destiny of that being. But it also depends on the type of being. Specifically, only a higher being, which possesses an existence that is more rounded and more harmoniously self-contained within itself, can sustain and requires the spherical form. Not a pure sphere, of course, as that would contradict all <term>individualization<note>The process by which a general form becomes a specific, unique individual.</note></term>; but it suffices that the principal feature is spherical, and that it allows for and possesses its own variations. The still rather complex primary form of man proves by itself that his organization is still far from an independent conclusion and the goal of perfection; rather, he belongs to the organs of elaboration, the

<summary>Fechner argues that the spherical shape of the Earth indicates it is a "higher being" more perfect than humans, whose complex and "entangled" forms suggest they are merely subordinate parts of a larger whole.</summary>

means of completion; rather than being something complete in himself. And should he not be modest enough not to contradict this? Yet, in his form, there appear tendencies toward a certain "rounding off," which become most significant at those points that are most meaningful to us. What the Earth can achieve, but man as a whole cannot, we see him approximately achieve in his noblest parts—the **head** and the **eye**—which rise most prominently above their dependence, not from the Earth itself, but from the lowly ground. Thus, we have first the Earth itself, then the human head within it, and the human eye within that as approximations of the <term>sphere<note>original: "Kugel." In Fechner’s worldview, the sphere is the geometric expression of a "higher being" that is self-contained and spiritually complete.</note></term>; however, the head signifies more than the eye, and the Earth signifies more than the head. 

From <term>teleological perspectives<note>Teleology is the study of purpose or design in nature. Fechner is arguing that the human form is "designed" the way it is because of our physical limitations, whereas the Earth's form reflects its higher purpose.</note></term>, it can be assumed that man, in terms of his form, would have become entirely head or eye—thereby reflecting the Earth even more purely upon the Earth than is currently the case—if only he could have existed completely without dependence on the ground. Earlier, the spherical shape of the Earth was teleologically linked to its external independence and its <term>lack of material need<note>original: "Bedürfnißlosigkeit." This refers to the idea that the Earth does not need to "consume" outside matter in the way animals do, as it is a self-sustaining system.</note></term>. (Vol. I, p. 106, 242). Therefore, what distinguishes the human form from that of the Earth is to be understood merely as an expression of the lesser independence and completion of his being.

If the Earth is in its entirety what we are only in our most perfect parts, it is also far more perfect than those parts themselves. For—

### B. On the Solid Framework of the Earth

In a certain sense, the <term>rocky framework<note>original: "Felsgerüst." A term used here to describe the Earth's crust as a foundational structure similar to a building or a body.</note></term> of the Earth could be compared to the <term>skeletal framework<note>original: "Knochengerüst."</note></term> of the human body, insofar as it serves the Earth as a solid foundation for the attachment of movable parts, just as the skeleton serves us. From another perspective, however, our own skeleton can be seen as a movable part of the <term>Earth-skeleton<note>original: "Erdskelet."</note></term>—as an articulated limb—since the voluntary movement of our body in relation to the <term>Earth-body<note>original: "Erdkörper."</note></term> can only occur by virtue of being anchored to it, much like the voluntary movement of our own limbs in relation to the rest of our body (cf. Part I, p. 115); many other points of equivalence arise here. Our body is even more firmly and securely joined to the main body of the Earth—while simultaneously allowing for greater freedom of movement—than any limb of our body is to its trunk. In fact, <term>gravity<note>original: "Schwere." In nineteenth-century natural philosophy, gravity was often described as a binding force that "fettered" organisms to the planet, acting as a functional equivalent to joints and ligaments.</note></term> keeps the human being more tightly bound to the Earth and returns him more surely to it when he attempts to leave it, than all the elastic...

We find here, as so often, an advantage that the <term>human organization<note>original: "Organisation des Menschen." Man, the highest creature on Earth, surpasses all animals that possess a **skeleton** in the ability to turn and rotate his **limbs** in all directions; but the Earth surpasses him beyond measure by employing him, along with the other animals, as its own movable limbs. The <term>Weber brothers<note>original: "Gebrüder Weber." In the same way, the <term>Earth-body<note>original: "Erdkörper."</note></term> can reach any part of itself by means of human beings, with the possible exception of the extreme <term>polar regions<note>original: "Polargegenden."</note></term>, and it does so with much freer movement and in much more manifold ways than are available to us with our arms.

It does not possess the full nature of a fixed foundational framework at all; rather, it is more or less shaken and bent during all movements of our limbs. This, however, causes no harm, because the Earth remains firm. The Earth owes to this powerful preponderance of its foundational framework over its mobile limb-parts the great independence with which it can move them. No matter how many people and animals tread upon it, not one wobbles because of the step of another; instead, each person performs their own movement safely and undisturbed by the movements of others, through their <term>joint-connection<note>original: "Gelenkverbindung." Here we see once again how the great similarity between the conditions of man and Earth in one respect fails completely in another. Nothing can be more comparable, in a certain sense, than the <term>articulation<note>original: "Einlenkung." But here, as everywhere, we find that the Earth’s deviation from the human model serves a <term>higher expediency<note>original: "höhern Zweckmäßigkeit." A term in natural philosophy suggesting that nature’s designs are optimized for a specific, often divine, purpose.</note></term>. 

If we demanded—in order to compare humans and animals perfectly with the limbs of the Earth—that they be as large in proportion to the planet as our own limbs are in proportion to our main trunk, we would also be demanding that every step of a human or animal mightily shake the entire Earth. In such a case, all other people and animals would be shaken along with it. To prevent this, the Earth's "limbs" have been made tiny in proportion to the whole Earth; in this one respect, they are certainly no longer truly comparable to our own limbs. Otherwise, the observation made in **Volume I, page 73** regarding the higher significance of small variations finds its application here, as it will often in the following pages.
