<meta>This page transitions from the discussion of the Earth's solid crust—previously described as a vast graveyard of microscopic life—to the study of the Earth's "fluid" systems. It establishes a physiological parallel between the human body and the planet.</meta>

## C. On the Fluid Element of the Earth.

Just as the firm framework of our body can only fulfill its functions in dependence upon that of the Earth, by having to support itself upon it, so too the system of fluid-conducting vessels (<term>veins<note>original: "Adern." In this historical context, the author uses "veins" broadly to refer to any vessel carrying life-sustaining fluids, both in humans and by analogy in the Earth.</note></term>) in our body can only function in dependence upon that of the Earth, insofar as it must first draw its fluid from it and return it to it. Consequently, this system itself may be regarded as a complementary part of the Earth's own fluid system; for this very reason, it can no more be a simple repetition of the Earth's system than our firm <term>framework<note>original: "Gerüst." Refers here to the skeletal system.</note></term> is a repetition of the Earth's crust, with which it must instead combine to form a complete system.

Rivers and streams carry water downward; trees and herbs lift it upward; humans and animals carry it in every direction, moving it in a circle within themselves, and mixing and processing it with substances that no stream or tree can reach. Rivers and streams are channels open at the top, pouring into vast lakes and the sea with a free view toward the heavens, in order to return as much as possible and as quickly as possible to the clouds. The trees, which seek to lift the water, lead it upward from the hiding places of the soil in closed, compressed <term>sap tubes<note>original: "Saftröhren." An early botanical term for the vascular tissues (xylem and phloem) that transport water and nutrients through a plant.</note></term>, encased in firm bark, so as not to evaporate too much of it along the way. Only at the top, when it can go no higher, do they spread out into branches, leaves, and needles, in order to [release] it as quickly as from the nozzle of a <term>watering can<note>original: "Gießkanne."</note></term> and—

...as easily as possible as vapor, and in exchange, to pump up new water from below. Our respiratory organs are relatively small branches of the Earth's respiratory organ, just as our skeletons are branches of the great Earth-skeleton, and our fluid-carrying vessels are branches of the great sea—and for analogous reasons. If the atmosphere were not such a vast **respiratory reservoir**, our breathing organs would not find the security for the constant satisfaction of their respiratory needs that they find now. There would be a lack of the right quantity here, and the right quality of air there. The atmosphere shows particularly beautifully what we see everywhere in our own organism: that within an organically linked whole, the same part reveals purposeful relationships not just in one direction, but in all directions.

As a respiratory tool, it is at the same time the most universal vocal tool. One can find a kind of miracle in how the atmosphere combines such seemingly opposite properties; it is the lightest and most mobile of things, facilitating the slightest movements, yet it is simultaneously the most persistent, uniform, and steady weight upon our Earth—wing and press in one. <note>Fechner uses the "wing" to symbolize the air's lightness and the "press" (as in a mechanical or printing press) to symbolize its immense weight.</note> What could seem more different than these functions? Just as the Earth in general contains much within itself that we often look for outside of ourselves, so too does it possess in the atmosphere an organ for many accomplishments for which we would otherwise have to provide our own external tools.

When a patch of plant growth had, so to speak, swallowed its fill of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and was able to gain nothing more from it—rather, starting to return just as much carbon dioxide to the air through decaying parts as it drew from it during its ongoing growth—it was buried beneath the earth, and a new vegetation grew over it, continuing the work of air purification. We have found 50, 60, even up to 120 coal seams <term>Steinkohlenlager: distinct layers of coal found within the earth, each representing a submerged ancient forest</term> layered one above the other, each of which could only have gained its carbon through the absorption and decomposition of carbon dioxide. Since in earlier times there were no such large-scale means of destroying the plant world by the animal and human worlds as there are now—for cattle and sheep did not yet graze the land, and humans did not yet burn or consume the wood of the forests—destruction through natural revolutions <note>The author refers to "Naturrevolutionen," a 19th-century geological concept suggesting that the Earth's history was shaped by sudden, catastrophic events that wiped out species and reshaped the landscape.</note> was the only means of obtaining constantly young vegetation in sufficiently rapid succession.

But it was not only the land, but also the sea with its creatures that helped toward the same purpose, although in quite a different way. The sea, you see, initially swallowed its share of carbon dioxide as well; however, to keep the sea perpetually thirsty for it, the carbon dioxide was repeatedly removed from the water through the formation of the calcareous shells <note>original: "Kalkschalen"; shells made of calcium carbonate</note> of lower creatures, as these essentially consist of carbo- <note>The text cuts off here, likely continuing with "carbonates."</note>

...consisting of <term>carbonate of lime: calcium carbonate, the primary component of limestone and shells</term>, withdrawn from the sea; these were also buried again and again, so that they now form chalk deposits up to 500 feet thick.

But now, if it had always continued in this way, the plants and animals would have eventually swallowed all the carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, and nothing would have remained for the further nourishment of the former or for the formation of new shells for the latter. The Earth, therefore, had to finally begin to restrain its waste of carbon dioxide and start a new economy in order to produce an equally strong abundance of life with a reduced expenditure of carbon dioxide. Accordingly, it no longer buried plants as it had before, but instead left them more to gradual decay on the surface, whereby their carbon returns to the air. Secondly, to compensate for the amount of sea creatures—which was necessarily decreasing on its own as carbon dioxide levels fell—that required calcium carbonate for their solid skeletons, it increased the number of higher animal species whose skeletons consist of <term>phosphate of lime: calcium phosphate, the main structural component of bones in vertebrates</term>. Thirdly, through their method of feeding and breathing, it directed the newly created creatures more than the earlier ones to convert the carbon of the plants they consumed back into carbon dioxide and return it to the atmosphere*;

Only with warm-blooded animals—that is, birds and mammals—does a vigorous respiratory process begin.

## E. On the Imponderable Powers.

In his nerves, man possesses a mysterious **agent**; at least it is suspected that, besides the protein-like matter of which they consist, a fine, <term>imponderable: a term used in 18th and 19th-century science for substances or forces—like heat, light, or electricity—that were thought to have no detectable weight</term> medium of an unknown nature is contained within them. If this is the case, it can only be the highest earthly organized development or "bloom" of that same fine medium which, as the general foundation of the **imponderable powers**, permeates and surrounds heaven and earth, but in the earthly realm is bound and moved in specific ways. 

Or how else did it first enter into man? It is best to make no further hypotheses about this agent—which is itself merely hypothetical—but rather to be satisfied with this general viewpoint. Otherwise, the imponderable occurs in many other **modifications** upon and within the earth, the origin and connection of which we partly know and partly do not know, although—

One might ask: what is the purpose of the internal Earth heat and its protection? The same barrier that the solid Earth's crust <term>Earth's crust (Erdkruste): the outermost solid shell of our planet</term> presents to the escape of heat from the Earth also ensures that the heat from the interior is no longer felt on the surface; instead, the surface's warmth now depends perceptibly only on the external influence of the sun. Thus, it might seem useless to retain the heat in the interior—perhaps even counterproductive—since it is precisely this retention that renders the heat useless for the surface. In earlier times, the heat still reached the Earth's surface perceptibly or was renewed upon it by the upwelling of hot mountain masses. Furthermore, the sealing of the **internal heat** from the outside is not so complete that local additions of heat from the inside to the outside do not occur in deep cellars and mines, in hot springs, **artesian wells** <term>artesischen Brunnen</term> <note>A well where water rises to the surface under internal pressure without needing a pump.</note>, and probably also the **Gulf Stream**, which serve their purpose; and naturally, the sustained flow of these useful heat sources depends on the heat not dissipating rapidly and from all sides of the Earth.

The **Gulf Stream**, whose water is heated up to 31° C in the Gulf of Mexico, contributes significantly as it turns toward Europe to mildening the European climate. Through the influence of this current, Northern Europe is separated from the belt of polar ice by an ice-free sea; even in the coldest times, the boundary of the polar ice does not reach the European coasts. <meta>This page continues the discussion on the Earth’s internal energies. While the previous page focused on the physical "leaks" of internal heat (hot springs, mines), this page transitions into the mystery of terrestrial magnetism and the philosophical distinction between "self-luminosity" and "internal warmth."</meta>

...[period]ic changes it undergoes can only owe their origin to a mobile or moving cause, and beyond the utility it has for **navigation** <term>Schifffahrt</term> and **surveying** <term>Feldmesskunst</term>, it may have a more general significance for the Earth, over which as much darkness lies as over the actual reason for its origin.

The changes in **terrestrial magnetism** <term>Erdmagnetismus</term> according to the time of day and season are indisputably connected with the path of the sun; by contrast, the cause of **secular variations** <term>secularen Veränderungen</term> <note>Long-term changes in the Earth's magnetic field that occur over centuries rather than daily cycles.</note> can hardly be sought anywhere but in the Earth's interior.

To seek the cause of terrestrial magnetism itself in a **magnetic iron core**, as has often been done, is hindered partly by this internal variability, which would be difficult to trace back to mere temperature changes in a solid core, and partly by the fact that iron generally loses its magnetism when glowing hot. Iron in the interior, however, as far as we must believe, could only exist in a glowing, fluid state.

Indisputably, the Earth was formerly entirely glowing and fluid, and also **self-luminous** <term>selbstleuchtend</term>, just as it is still **self-warming** <term>selbstwarm</term>. But this self-luminosity, occurring only at the surface at very high temperatures, expired earlier than the internal heat, which found refuge in the interior. With few exceptions, living creatures are also not self-luminous, whereas many possess their own **body heat** <term>Eigenwärme</term>. Light on the surface of the Earth now depends, just like heat, mainly on the sun; however, in the moon, the Earth has an auxiliary apparatus for the illumination of the nights, without a corresponding auxiliary apparatus for the warming of the nights, since moonlight—though not cooling as was formerly thought <note>There was a historical folk belief and some early scientific speculation that moonlight had a "frigorific" or cooling quality.</note>—acts only imperceptibly as a source of heat. This can be interpreted **teleologically** <note>Teleology is the study of purpose or design in nature; the author suggests that the moon provides light without heat because that serves a specific biological or planetary purpose.</note>.

In the lungs, the furnace of our body has a never-resting **bellows** <term>Blasbalg</term>, which draws in useful air with every inhalation and expels useless air with every exhalation; however, it has no **chimney** <term>Esse</term> <note>The author uses the term "Esse," which refers specifically to the flue or chimney of a forge or furnace designed to create a draft and remove smoke.</note>, because its perfect design makes one unnecessary. ...our furnace does not stand still, but rather runs after its **fuel**; it also possesses in its teeth the tools to prepare the material by breaking it down, since—just as with our firewood—the heating power increases through more complete reduction. <meta>This page continues the discussion of physiological heat regulation, specifically detailing experimental data on breathing rates and the physical mechanisms the body uses to maintain a stable internal temperature despite seasonal or environmental changes.</meta>

...in the number and depth of breaths, as well as in the **carbon dioxide content** <term>Kohlensäuregehalt</term> of the exhaled air. At a temperature of 8.47° C, **Vierordt** <note>Karl von Vierordt (1818–1884), a German physiologist who pioneered methods for measuring blood flow and respiratory gases.</note> breathed 12.16 times per minute; at 19.40° C, he breathed only 11.57 times. At 8.47° C, he exhaled 299.33 cc of carbon dioxide; at 19.40° C, only 257.81 cc.
->(Wagner’s Dictionary of Physiology, Art. Digestion, p. 667).<-

**Edwards** <note>William Frédéric Edwards (1777–1842), a French physiologist known for his work on the influence of environmental factors on animal life.</note> has demonstrated through numerous comparative experiments on small birds—sparrows, yellowhammers, and siskins—that even when the temperature is artificially equalized, they breathe less and produce less heat in summer than in winter. This can only depend on the fact that the physical constitution changes accordingly from summer to winter. One can conclude from several circumstances that the same applies to humans. (Edwards, *On the Influence of Physical Agents on Life*, etc. p. 163, 200, 487).

In addition, however, the following aids contribute very significantly to maintaining the uniformity of temperature:

1) In the heat, **evaporation** <term>Ausdünstung</term> <note>The author refers to both perspiration and the moisture lost through breathing.</note> increases; however, through evaporation, heat is "bound" <note>This refers to latent heat; the physical process where liquid turning into vapor consumes energy, thereby cooling the body.</note> or cooling is generated; in the cold, evaporation and therefore cooling decreases.

2) In the heat, the blood moves more toward the skin, as evidenced by the swelling of the veins; in the cold, it moves more inward. In the former case, the blood is more exposed to cooling by the external atmosphere (for even very warm air is generally still colder than 30° R <note>30° Réaumur is approximately 37.5° Celsius or 99.5° Fahrenheit—the standard internal body temperature.</note>), while in the latter, it is more withdrawn from it.

3) As the skin cools due to external cold, the temperature difference between the skin and the air becomes smaller, and thus the **heat radiation** <term>Wärmestrahlung</term>, which depends on the magnitude of this temperature difference, is reduced.

It also outlines three physical mechanisms for heat regulation: evaporation, blood shunting to or from the skin, and changes in heat radiation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the physiological mechanisms used to regulate body temperature, specifically concluding a numbered list of biological adaptations before transitioning to the external resources provided by the Earth to assist human survival.</meta>

4) The **layers of fat** <term>Fettlagen</term> beneath the skin are very poor conductors of heat.

Through the combination of all these means, it follows that humans maintain their internal temperature nearly constant, even though the temperature at the skin fluctuations considerably according to the external temperature (just as the same principle applies to the entire Earth). <note>Fechner frequently draws parallels between the physiology of the human body and the "physiology" of the Earth, a core theme of his work *Zend-Avesta*, which argues that the Earth is a living, ensouled being.</note>

Meanwhile, the effectiveness of these means has its limits. If the cold becomes too extreme, a person freezes to death, and if the heat becomes too intense, they burn regardless. However, these natural aids are sufficient for the average conditions found in the habitable parts of the Earth; furthermore, the Earth offers a great variety of external resources that allow humans to compensate for even unusual environmental influences and to expand the limits of the Earth's habitability. One may observe, however, that the Earth provides many more—or at least more powerful—external resources against cold than against heat. This is related to the fact that heat on Earth rarely, if ever, rises above a level that can be tolerated, whereas cold often does (partly toward the poles, partly on high mountains, and partly during winter). For protection against intense heat, we have little more than shade, ventilation, cool dwellings, and cold drinks; for protection against cold, however, we have not only the counterparts to those—sheltered and still locations, warm dwellings, and hot or stimulating drinks—but also very diverse and powerful...

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s discussion of the external resources provided by the Earth to help humans regulate their temperature. The previous page ended mid-sentence, discussing resources against the cold such as sheltered locations, dwellings, and drinks.</meta>

...in fuel materials, warm clothing, and bedding, whereas the protection that artificially stored ice or mountain ice grants against heat is of less importance, as it is difficult to obtain.

There are also several specific <term>teleological remarks</term> <note>Teleology is the study of design or purpose in nature; Fechner suggests that the Earth's resources are "designed" to meet the needs of living beings.</note> to be made here. Just as Nature keeps a reservoir of cooling in the form of ice and snow upon the heights, she has kept a reservoir of fuel in the form of **coal** <term>Steinkohlen</term> in the depths. Many means that serve for cooling in summer can, in another respect, also serve for warming <note>The original German text repeats "in summer" here, though the context of the comparison with winter suggests this is a scribal error for "in winter."</note>, such as deep cellars or houses with thick walls. Forests provide shade in the summer and firewood for the winter, and so on.

It is interesting to observe how the **organic furnace** <note>Fechner uses this metaphor to describe the body's metabolic heat production, comparing biological respiration to the combustion in a stove.</note> adapts itself according to the different conditions under which it is destined to operate. We have previously considered the influence of body size in this regard (Part I, p. 84). If the furnace is to be surrounded by water, as is the case with **seals** and **whales**, a disadvantageous circumstance must be overcome: dense water draws away incomparably more heat in the same amount of time than thin air does. This requires special precautions. Accordingly, such animals are padded with very thick **layers of fat** beneath the skin; furthermore, the **respiratory process** <term>Athmungsproceß</term> is exceptionally developed, at least in seals (according to **E. H. Weber** <note>Ernst Heinrich Weber (1795–1878), a prominent German physician and colleague of Fechner at the University of Leipzig, known for his work on anatomy and physiology.</note>). This is not so much the case with whales; however, their enormous size contributes to keeping them warm. In general, the processes of heat generation and heat preservation are determined by a cooperation of many circumstances that can more or less substitute for one another. Since the organism has many other purposes to fulfill besides generating and preserving heat, a specific means may sometimes conflict with another purpose the organism must fulfill; in such cases, Nature relies on a different method.

<meta>This page follows the discussion of the physical and biological means by which heat is regulated, specifically continuing from the previous page's mention of how organic "furnaces" like whales and seals adapt to their environment. Fechner now transitions to a broader physical principle: how the Earth itself "cooperates" with the Sun to produce warmth.</meta>

Regarding the heat that the Earth receives through the mediation of the Sun, we are easily inclined to assign too passive a role to the Earth, as if the heat flowed onto it, so to speak, ready-made. Fundamentally, however, the warming of the Earth in the sunshine is an internal act of its surface, merely stimulated by the Sun, much like how the twitching of a muscle certainly requires an external stimulus to arise, and results in different ways and different intensities according to how and how strongly that stimulus is applied; yet it always remains the muscle's own action <note>Fechner uses this physiological analogy to argue that heat is not just "delivered" to Earth, but is a product of the Earth's specific physical reaction to solar radiation.</note>. This can be easily proven. The higher one rises in a hot-air balloon or on a high mountain, the more one freezes, even though the sunbeams reach him more directly <note>original: "unverkürzter" – meaning the rays have traveled through less of the atmosphere and are therefore less diminished.</note> than below. Why? The opaque surface of the Earth is necessary to "entice" the heat from the sunbeams. This heat then rises with the air or the water, which are warmed at the ground, and thus certainly reaches higher altitudes to a greater or lesser degree; but in themselves, neither water nor air, being transparent bodies, are capable of heating up in a sunbeam—or they can only do so insofar as they lack perfect transparency. If one places water in the focus of a **burning mirror** <note>A concave mirror used to concentrate sunlight into a single point of intense heat.</note> in which even the most **refractory metals** <term>strengflüssigsten Metalle</term> <note>Metals with very high melting points that are difficult to liquefy.</note> melt, the water will not even boil; **ether** <note>A highly volatile and flammable liquid used in 19th-century physics experiments.</note> does not ignite in it. In contrast, every opaque body warms up under the influence of the Sun, and indeed each one differently under the same solar influence, depending on its own composition: black bodies more strongly than white ones, rough ones more strongly than smooth ones.

It is no different with illumination and coloration than it is with warming. The Earth must cooperate actively in this process; the sunbeams bring only the stimulus. A body appears illuminated only because it reflects light through its own inherent forces; and depending on how it does so, it appears black, white, or colored. Sunlight does not paint bodies the way we paint something with a brush—which brings along a specific, ready-made color for every spot—but rather, bodies must paint themselves with their preferred color from the general "paint pot" <note>original: "Farbentopfe." This metaphor emphasizes that sunlight contains all colors (white light), but the object decides which part of the spectrum to reflect.</note> of sunlight. The entire colorful landscape with which the Earth is covered is, from a certain perspective, the Earth's own work, though certainly not its work alone. Even the blue of the sky is, from this perspective, only an earthly blue. The air creates the blue color for itself out of the colorless light of the heavens. <note>Fechner is describing the phenomenon where the atmosphere scatters light to create the blue sky, suggesting that the "blue" is a property of our atmosphere's interaction with light rather than a property of space itself.</note>

## F. On the Development of the Earth.

Our own organism, and every animal and plant organism, develops out of a relatively uniform mass and a monotony of conditions in such a way that, over time, it becomes increasingly structured and subdivided, developing ever more multifaceted relationships both internally and externally. It is not without interest to follow the analogous course of development in the Earth, although here only hypotheses are at our disposal—which, however, in part possess a high degree of probability. <note>This marks a transition from physics to "natural history" or cosmogony, where Fechner applies the biological principle of "differentiation" (moving from simple to complex) to the history of the entire planet.</note>

<meta>This page transitions from the general principle of the Earth as an active, self-organizing entity to a specific scientific cosmogony. Based on all that we can conclude, the Earth behaves like a sphere that has gradually cooled down from a very high temperature. If we trace this cooling process <term>cooling process (Erkaltungsproceß)</term> back as far as possible using probable inferences <term>probable inferences (Wahrscheinlichkeitsschlüsse)</term>, there was a time when even the most viscous <note>original: "schwerflüssigsten," referring to substances with extremely high melting points that are difficult to liquefy.</note> earthly bodies were still molten. Looking even further back, there was a time when even the most fire-resistant <note>original: "feuerbeständigsten," or refractory substances that resist melting or vaporization.</note> bodies were vaporized. In a word, there was a time when the entire Earth represented nothing but a monstrous sphere of glowing, dense vapor, in which there could not yet be any talk of a distinct separation of substances, since vapors mix together uniformly.

Gradually, however, this sphere cooled, and a portion of it—containing the less volatile substances—condensed into a large, liquid <note>original: "tropfbar flüssig," literally "liquid capable of forming drops," used here to describe the transition from gas to a molten state.</note> but still glowing sphere. Because of its greater density, this sphere took the central position and was surrounded by a very hot envelope of gas or vapor. The liquid sphere mainly contained metallic and earthy substances in a molten state. The gaseous or vaporous envelope, however, contained—in addition to the atmospheric air—all the water that is currently on the Earth, since the hot surface of the condensed sphere did not yet permit any precipitation of water vapors into liquid form. It also contained all the carbonic acid <note>original: "Kohlensäure." In the scientific context of the time, this refers to carbon dioxide (CO2).</note> and other acids which, in intense heat, can only exist in gaseous or vaporous form. Thus, the single mass had divided itself into two: a liquid central mass and a gaseous or vaporous envelope.

One can certainly represent the beginning of this development somewhat differently; however, as to the later progress <note>The sentence ends abruptly here at the bottom of the page.</note>

> “The other cause that can be given for this acceleration <term>acceleration (Beschleunigung)</term> lies in the tail <term>tail (Schweif)</term> that comets usually display. This consists of extremely light matter <term>matter (Materie)</term> which the comet drives away from itself, and which usually recedes in the direction opposite to the Sun; it is very easy to overlook that the comet cannot exert a force in any direction without itself experiencing the counter-reaction of this force in the opposite direction; the tail flowing away from the comet, which we see, thus shows us that the comet itself is driven toward the Sun by another force besides its gravitational attraction, and must therefore move differently than it would if it were subject to that force alone. This cause, too, must produce an acceleration of the movement. Which of the two causes is the one actually present, or whether both are present simultaneously, we do not yet know; even less can we know how strongly these causes affect the comet.”

We cannot explain the first origin <term>origin (Entstehung)</term> of organic beings—that is, we cannot make it dependent on the principles of processes known to us today. Insofar as we are concerned here only with the material side of organic creations <term>creations (Schöpfungen)</term>, this proposition can be narrowed even further for our purpose: that different types of material effects always require different types of material causes. <meta>This page continues the discussion on the origins of life, moving from the arguments for gradual evolution (the "first view") to the "other view" which emphasizes the Earth's own creative agency and the limits of biological adaptation.</meta>

## Reasons for the Other View

What boldness it takes to imagine man as having been developed out of infusoria <note>infusoria: a historical term for microscopic organisms like ciliates found in organic infusions</note>, polyps <note>polyps: simple, sedentary aquatic animals such as coral or anemones</note>, or at most fish*? Here, every analogy fails. While the constitution of animals can currently be modified within certain limits by changing external circumstances, if one goes beyond these limits, the creatures waste away and die out—quickly or slowly, depending on whether the change is attempted quickly or slowly. No fact exists to suggest that even the slowest modification of conditions could expand the limits of organic change indefinitely.

Furthermore, the emergence of new beings seems to have been related not so much to slow changes as to rapid upheavals <note>original: *Umwälzungen*; Fechner refers here to the geological theory of "catastrophism," which suggested that sudden, violent events changed the Earth's history</note>, which simultaneously brought about the destruction of the old and the conditions for the emergence of the new. One may indeed harbor doubts about this, yet it remains the most probable scenario. 

Much more plausible and less difficult than the assumption of a direct emergence of higher creatures from lower ones is the assumption of a **further development of the creative activity of the Earth itself**. In this way, the "leap" [between species] is avoided, but in a different manner. Even our spinning machine did not emerge from earlier spinning wheels, nor our English grand pianos <note>original: *englischen Flügel*; the modern grand piano was often referred to as a "wing" due to its shape</note> from earlier pianos in such a way that the earlier instruments were themselves rebuilt; rather, the latter were set aside and the new instruments

<meta>This page continues the philosophical argument from page 188, transitioning from the physical durability of the first humans to their survival through natural instincts provided by the Earth and their eventual transition into a state of reason.</meta>

...whose dangers they did not know how to ward off. Indeed, if the first humans had been born like children today and placed in the forest or a meadow in the cold among wild animals—as a human mother might do if she forgot her maternal duties—then their situation would have looked precarious. But in general, the mother cares for the child, and the child knows how to find the breast. In the same way, the Earth itself must have cared directly for its child, the first human; since the Earth had not yet produced a mother to care for grandchildren, it would have placed them in the most favorable location, and man would have possessed his instincts that allowed him to find what was necessary on Earth, just as a child today has instincts to find what is necessary from its human mother. These **primordial instincts** <term>Urinstincte: the innate, natural impulses present at the very beginning of human existence, before the development of learned culture</term>, however, were lost as generations descended further and multiplied—partly because the human origin, sinking ever deeper into the human realm, brought different consequences than the first divine origin, and partly because these instincts became less necessary as humans received help from other humans and developed their reason more fully. The first **golden age** <note>A mythical period of primordial peace, harmony, and prosperity, often cited in classical and religious traditions</note> of humanity thus gradually vanished. In this way, the meeting of the **causal** <term>Causal: relating to the laws of cause and effect in the physical world</term> and the **teleological** <term>Teleological: the philosophical idea that nature and history have a design or specific purpose</term>, which we notice everywhere else, asserts itself here as well.

As is well known, the Bible portrays the first humans as being in an initially more perfect state and in more intimate communion with God than those born later; and in the myths of most nations, the first human is himself considered to be of a divine nature.

<meta>This page continues the philosophical argument following the quote from Alexander von Humboldt. What is it that makes us inclined to see in man, even now, the **king of the Earth** above all animals—even those that are otherwise very similar in appearance? It is the oversight, mastery, connection, and centering of all earthly conditions that are established in him and through him. 

But if we look closer, this [mastery] in man’s current constitution appears to be more of a path prepared or initiated than something truly achieved or achievable. In any case, it is brought about through extremely laborious means external to man <note>Fechner is referring to technology and external tools—like ships, bridges, or roads—which humans must build to compensate for the physical limitations of their own bodies.</note>, and it always remains highly fragmentary and incomplete. Every mountain, every river, every sea presents an obstacle that man only gradually learned to overcome, and even now overcomes only with the expenditure of time and effort. 

Yet if man himself devises ever better methods to aid him in these regards, without being able to fully overcome the **inadequacy** of his nature, should not Nature—who seems to "invent" in a manner quite similar to man—one day be able to overcome those inadequacies even more directly by perfecting her previous "human invention"? Especially since the means for this are close at hand. Should she not, once the connection and relationship of earthly conditions has been brought by man as far as is possible according to his nature, bring about a new and higher **progress** by elevating his nature itself, or by producing a higher nature above his own? For man, according to his nature, cannot push beyond a certain **limit**. Even man, when he [seeks/creates] more perfect...

<meta>This page continues the argument that human development may not be the final stage of evolution. I must admit that one circumstance in particular has always seemed questionable to me regarding the view of man as the final conclusion of earthly-organic development. Man considers himself the highest creature, yet the bird flies high above him. To me, this does not seem to be a satisfying conclusion, neither from an aesthetic nor a **teleological** <note>Teleology is the study of purpose or design in nature; Fechner is arguing that if nature has a design, leaving the most "rational" being grounded while "lesser" beings fly seems like an unfinished plan.</note> perspective. Only the wing of the bird would provide an adequate material tool for man's **reason** <note>In this context, "reason" (Vernunft) refers to the human capacity to understand the world as a whole and perceive the connections between all things.</note>—which strives to survey, fly over, and connect everything from above—enabling it to practically satisfy its highest tasks. His hands, with which he rules the Earth, would, so to speak, be extended by as much distance as his wings could carry him. The bird certainly has wings, but because it possesses neither the reason nor the hands of man, all those advantages are of little use to it. Only for a rational being can the wing develop its greatest possible potential, and likewise, only by means of the wing can reason reach its greatest possible power...

For however little a bat may otherwise seem to resemble a human, it has nevertheless—due to significant similarities in dental structure and the position of the breasts—been united with humans and monkeys into a special order, which was placed at the head of all other animals, as was done by Linnaeus <note>Carl Linnaeus (1707–1778), the Swedish scientist who created the system of biological classification we use today. He grouped humans, monkeys, and bats together in the order *Primates*</note>. And since there were already prehistoric <note>original: "vorweltliche"; literally "pre-world," referring to extinct species from previous geological epochs</note> monkeys and bats, one can see in them a kind of prelude to humanity.

These animals have therefore already made more progress in rising above the ground than humans, and they seem to suggest that as nature approached humans in its process of development <note>original: "Bildungsgange"; the 19th-century idea of an unfolding plan of nature</note>, it was truly intent on initiating an even more complete elevation. In the meantime, however, the mastery of the ground could not be achieved in the monkey or the bat despite their freer elevation above it. This mastery is secured for humans through the combination of their hands and their upright posture, aided by reason <note>original: "Vernunft"</note>; accordingly, nature preferred to give up some of that advantage of free elevation in the case of humans, and instead applied all its diligence to the development of the brain and the formation of the hand and the foot, in order to use the latter—

<meta>This page continues the author’s exploration of human anatomy and the trade-offs of the "structural plan" of living beings. Fundamentally, humans acknowledge the advantage that the possession of wings would provide by depicting angels—who are otherwise entirely human in form—with wings. Of course, something is not as easily created as it is painted. If humans were actually to receive wings, they could not simply be attached as a painter does; the entire structural plan <note>original: "Organisationsplan"; referring to the underlying biological blueprint or architecture of a species</note> would have to change. When we observe nature's process of development <note>original: "Bildungsgang"</note>, an obvious conflict arises in the task of providing strong legs, hands, and wings all at once. 

In birds, wings are not added onto four feet or onto two hands and two feet; rather, the two front limbs <note>original: "Extremitäten"</note> transform themselves into wings, and because of this, the bird loses out on the advantages of having hands. In insects, wings occur alongside several pairs of legs; however, a caterpillar has more legs than a butterfly. Even here, the wings seem to have developed at the expense of legs; furthermore, a butterfly's legs are weak and thin and cannot replace hands. The actual tools for manipulation <note>original: "Handthieren"; an older term for handling, managing, or working with the hands</note> are located more on the head in these creatures and are of a delicate nature. 

It is easy to understand why wings cannot easily exist in combination with strong arms and legs. Wings require powerful muscles and nerves for movement; strong arms and legs do as well. These structures compete for space, not just externally, but internally as well. That this is not necessary is proven by our own two eyes. An optical image of the same object falls into each of them, yet we see it as a single entity. **Insect eyes** prove it even more strikingly. One has been convinced through direct experiments that an object produces as many images in the eye of a fly as there are **facets** <term>facets: the individual hexagonal lenses that make up the compound eye of an insect</term> upon it; it is as if one views an object through an artificially faceted glass; but no one would believe that the fly truly sees the object that many times. 

Here we have on a small scale what may take place on a large scale with the Earth. <meta>This page continues Gustav Theodor Fechner’s argument that the Earth possesses a global "optical apparatus." On the previous page, he suggested that the sea acts as a mirror; here, he explains how its vast size and curvature function like a planetary-scale telescope.</meta>

Through the large radius of curvature and the size of the **convex mirror** <term>Convexspiegel: a mirror that curves outward, like the surface of a ball. Because the Earth is a sphere, its oceans form a massive, outward-curving mirror.</term> that the sea provides, two advantages are achieved simultaneously—advantages that we also seek by enlarging the mirrors or **objectives** <term>Objective: the primary lens or mirror in a telescope that gathers light.</term> in our **telescopes**. First, the image itself is made larger, so that more **details** <note>Original: "Particularitäten."</note> become distinguishable within it; second, it is made more light-intensive, so that these details can be recognized more clearly.

Undeniably, the Earth is thereby enabled to recognize the surface of the sun and its neighboring planets with relatively as much clarity as we recognize the face of a person standing directly opposite us. This is true even if it does not see them with quite as much clarity as it can recognize its own surface by means of its "earthly eyes" <note>Fechner refers to the eyes of humans and animals as the Earth's internal sensory organs for looking at itself.</note>. The **fixed stars**, which appear to us as mere points even under the strongest magnification, may expand into discs of light for the Earth, much as the sun appears to us; however, the Earth may not yet be able to perceive their specific details, as the Earth's "stage" <note>Fechner often writes about the hierarchy of souls; here he suggests the Earth, though a higher being than a human, has not yet reached a spiritual or physical stage high enough to "resolve" the details of distant stars.</note> is not yet high enough for that.

Even the finer arrangements of our own **optical apparatus** are repeated in the Earth, likely with increased perfection; or rather, conversely, the finer arrangements of the Earth's optical apparatus are repeated in our eyes. The density of the lens in our eyes increases from the outside toward the inside; the same is true for the lens of the **atmosphere**. The curved media in our eye deviate slightly from a purely spherical shape, tending toward the elliptical (and parabolic), in order to [correct] the [blurring] dependent on **spherical aberration** <term>sphärische Abweichung: a phenomenon where light rays hitting the edges of a lens focus at a different point than those in the center, causing a blurry image.</term>...

<meta>This page continues Gustav Theodor Fechner's argument from page 226, where he suggests that the Earth acts as a giant optical instrument. The previous page discussed how the Earth's curvature helps resolve the details of celestial bodies like the sun and planets. This page addresses potential objections to this theory, such as the atmosphere's density and the roughness of the sea.</meta>

...to reduce clarity; likewise, the sea and the atmosphere deviate somewhat from a **spherical** shape toward an **elliptical** one, with varying degrees of elliptical curvature <note>Fechner is referring to the fact that the Earth is not a perfect sphere but an oblate spheroid, flattened at the poles.</note>. It would be of interest to one day calculate the optical effect of these circumstances more precisely. Since the atmosphere and sea must serve purposes other than the optical <note>For example, sustaining life, regulating climate, and enabling transport.</note>, it cannot be claimed that everything is calculated solely and specifically for an optical goal; rather, it is possible that in the **conflict** of purposes, the optical one may have had to yield here and there. But we have otherwise found so many instances where the Earth, through its systems on a grand scale, knows how to fulfill the most diverse purposes simultaneously and with equal perfection, resolving conflicts most happily—conflicts that persist in our own small-scale designs—that we would find it improbable if a significant conflict between different purposes were to remain here.

The fact that the atmosphere thins out so gradually is not a matter of indifference. For if the atmosphere were bounded by a dense layer, an image would arise and could be perceived through its reflective effect—following the same principle as the **surface of the sea**—and one image would interfere with the other. That the sea produces **waves**, and is therefore not smooth like a **mirror**, is of no consequence given its vast size. The small irregularities of our most perfect mirrors are undeniably, by comparison, far more significant than those created by waves on the surface of the sea.

Our eye is connected to a brain, and every fiber of the **retina** is linked with a brain fiber. This enables us not only to look, but also to **contemplate** what is seen. <meta>This page continues Fechner’s anatomical and philosophical comparison between the human eye and the Earth. Our eye is beautifully adorned with luster and color—indeed, adorned with luster and color more than any other part of our body; the Earth is adorned with luster and color even more beautifully; she is adorned with luster and color all the way around.

Our eye is gifted with a rolling movement <note>Fechner uses the term "rolling movement" (rollende Bewegung) to draw a direct anatomical parallel between the physical rotation of the eyeball in its socket and the rotation of the Earth on its axis.</note> in order to always present itself appropriately to earthly objects; the Earth is gifted with an even more perfect rolling movement in order to always present itself appropriately to heavenly objects <term>heavenly objects: In Fechner's worldview, these are the celestial bodies—stars, planets, and the sun—which the Earth "observes" as it rotates through space.</term>, and is capable of achieving something even more perfect thereby. But since the heavenly external conditions are simpler and more regular than our earthly ones, the rolling movement of the Earth could also be simpler and more regular than that of our eye.

Our eyes sleep half the time and wake half the time; here, too, they are only half of what the Earth is fully—for she <note>Fechner consistently personifies the Earth as a living, female being.</note> sleeps on one side and wakes on the other at the same time.

Where the sun is most powerful, so too is the growth of plants. But the sunbeam, passing into the void, would remain idle, colorless, and powerless. ...[cannot] produce a tone of a definite pitch. For us, the presence of intervening air is required so that we may hear something from another. For the celestial bodies, however, this is not necessary. **Gravitation** replaces **air tension** <term>Luftspannung: a 19th-century term for atmospheric pressure or the elastic property of air that allows it to transmit sound waves.</term> (insofar as the tides depend upon it), differing from it only in that it represents a material relation of force from one **cosmic atom** <note>original: "Weltatom" — Fechner views planets and stars as the fundamental particles or "atoms" of the conscious universe.</note> to another, rather than from one air atom to another. Just as sight propagates through light, hearing propagates through **gravity** <note>original: "Schwere"</note> throughout cosmic space, to every place where a suitable organ for it is found. For, of course, gravity is just as inaudible on its own as air tension, and just as light is invisible. The body that it pulls must strike something in order to awaken the **sensation of hearing** <note>original: "Gehörempfindung"</note>, just as light must strike something to awaken the **sensation of sight**. Now, it is a matter of making arrangements so that this striking occurs in an orderly manner, dependent upon the movement of the stars...

...follows. Thus the land is there, so that the sea may strike against it.

Among the various **oscillations** <term>Oscillations: rhythmic back-and-forth movements. Fechner views the rising and falling of the tides as the physical "sound waves" the Earth perceives.</term> into which the sea is set by the **celestial bodies** <note>original: "Gestirne"</note>, the one dependent on the **Moon** has by far the greatest preponderance over all others; next is the one caused by the **Sun**, followed by those caused by the other **planets**; those caused by the **fixed stars** are imperceptible. The Earth, therefore, "hears" most from the cosmic body that is bound to it in the same system <note>The Moon.</note>; indeed, which can in a certain sense still be counted as part of it; next most from the Sun, then from the other planets; from the remaining fixed stars it hears nothing, because these belong to a higher sphere.

If one does not shy away from a somewhat contrived comparison, one can even compare the Earth, in the formal nature of its arrangement, to an **ear**—not to that of the most developed creatures, but of the simplest, just as the resemblance of the Earth to an **eye** occurs primarily with the simpler forms of the eye. But these simplest arrangements are utilized by the Earth in the most magnificent way. Nor do these two comparisons contradict each other, for the Earth is capable of representing the most diverse things united within itself.

Let us take the **hearing organ** of a **mollusk** <note>original: "Muschelthieres" — literally "shell-animal," likely referring to bivalves or similar invertebrates.</note>. It consists of a simple, nerve-rich sac or vesicle full of fluid, with a small round stone (**ear-stone** <term>Otolith: a small calcium carbonate structure found in the inner ear of many animals, used to sense gravity and movement.</term>) inside it. The little stone is constantly in a dancing motion, which depends on the action of delicate **cilia** <note>original: "Wimpern" — tiny hair-like structures.</note> that sit on the inner wall of the vesicle and, through some unknown force, are in constant flickering motion, whereby they whip the fluid in which the stone floats. In all lower animals, the hearing organ is arranged similarly, though in many animals, such as **snails**, several stones are present instead of a single one, and they often take on a crystalline quality.

<meta>This page concludes Gustav Fechner's physiological analogy comparing the Earth's structure to a primitive ear, specifically focusing on the "otolith" or ear-stone. Now we see in the Earth an arrangement that is, in its external form, somewhat similar. The round or crystalline **otolith** <term>Otolith: literally an "ear-stone"; in many animals, these small, hard structures in the inner ear help detect gravity and motion.</term> is the round, solid body of the Earth with its jagged land; the fluid is the sea; the nerve-rich envelope is the atmosphere, permeated with light and heat. There is no need for **cilia** <term>Cilia (original: Flimmerhaare): microscopic, hair-like structures that, in small organisms, vibrate to move fluid or sense movement.</term> to move the otolith and the fluid. The otolith moves by rotating, and the sea moves against it through the circulation of the **tide**. On a smaller scale, the sea is lashed by the winds.

It would be easy to extend these considerations even further, indeed even to put forward conjectures regarding the other senses. However, given the uncertainty of the subject, the preceding is enough—and perhaps already more than enough—to awaken a conception of how things might possibly be constituted in the higher **sensory sphere** <note>original: "Sinnlichkeitssphäre"</note>. We repeat: these considerations are not intended to be authoritative; rather, they are meant to indicate roughly in which direction the **point of view** <note>original: "Gesichtspunct"</note> of the observation might need to be elevated and expanded when it comes to ascending from the conditions that apply to our sensory life to the conditions of **superior beings** <note>Fechner refers to the Earth and other celestial bodies as "superior beings" (übergeordnete Wesen) possessing their own form of consciousness.</note>. In any case, an elevation and expansion is necessary here; yet for us, as subordinate beings, erring in this matter is also easily possible; this we readily and humbly admit.

## XVIII. Appendix to the Ninth Section.

### Additions regarding the Hierarchical Structure of the World.

If there are indeed many gradations of creatures in the "neighborly" sense of the higher to the lower <note>Fechner refers here to the "horizontal" hierarchy, comparing different species of animals or plants that exist alongside one another.</note>, then it is also quite conceivable that there are many gradations in that other sense—from the superior to the inferior * <margin>* In this appendix, I always use the terms "higher" and "lower," and "superior" and "inferior," in the sense of the distinction made in Part I, p. 320.</margin>. Given the greatness of God and the universe, we have no reason to be afraid. The organization of the divine **All** <note>original: "All" — the universe conceived as a single, divine totality.</note> certainly extends not only in breadth, but also in depth, from the top to the bottom.

Now, our **solar system** <term>Solar system (original: Sonnensystem): the Sun and the collection of planets and celestial bodies bound to it by gravity.</term> naturally presents itself as the next level above our Earth. Perhaps, at first glance, it may seem less self-contained on one hand, and more merged with the cosmic whole on the other, than our own bodies or the Earth. However, upon closer inspection, we find this is not the case.

Regarding the first point, all the movements of the planets are linked to one another through **mutual determination** <term>Mutual determination (original: Wechselbestimmtheit): the concept that every part of a system influences and is influenced by every other part, creating a unified whole.</term> and with—

# XIX. Appendix to the Eleventh Section.

## A. Practical Argument for the Existence of God and a Future Life.

->The argument from the agreement of the good and the true.<-
<note>original Latin: "Argumentum a consensu boni et veri"</note>

<meta>Continuing from the previous page's discussion of the supreme law of the world, where Fechner began to suggest that this law's significance is often overlooked despite being widely used in practice.</meta>

it seems to me that the fundamental significance, which belongs to it according to its universality and conceptual self-evidence for the entire realm of real existence, has not yet been sufficiently appreciated. Here follow several more discussions, partly to expand and partly to further detail those previously established. However, I will not enter once more into detail here regarding the relations of the law to the existence of the divine spirit <note>original: "göttlicher Geist"; Fechner refers to a conscious, universal soul animating the universe.</note>; since the earlier discussions were primarily concerned with this.

In both the realms of material and spiritual occurrences, we distinguish various laws; in the former, for example, that of gravitation, magnetic, electrical, and chemical attraction, the law of inertia <term>Beharrens: the tendency of an object to remain in its current state of motion or rest unless acted upon.</term>, the coexistence of small oscillations, and so on; in the latter, that of association, habituation, the linking of pleasure and drive, and so on. Many specific laws can be subordinated to a more general one; thus all specific laws of attraction are subordinate to the more general law that masses strive to move toward one another in the straight line connecting them, and all laws of attraction and repulsion simultaneously to the even more general law of **interaction** <term>Wechselwirkung: The principle of reciprocity or mutual influence between parts of a system.</term>, namely that masses generally strive to change their distance in the direction of their connecting line with equal quantities of motion <note>original: "Bewegungsquantitäten"; in modern physics, this relates to the conservation of momentum.</note>. The laws of association, habituation, and so on in the spiritual realm are themselves already general laws, to which specific laws for specific circumstances are subordinated, and which are in turn to be subordinated to even more general laws of spiritual occurrence.

<meta>Continuing from page 259, Fechner is expanding on the "Supreme World Law" and how it relates to both physical and mental phenomena by defining what constitutes a "general law."</meta>

It is easily apparent that the diversity of the **laws of occurrence** <note>original: *Geseze des Geschehens*</note> is just as much connected to the diversity of the circumstances for which they apply as it is to the diversity of the results <note>While *Erfolge* usually means "successes" today, in this scientific context it refers to "outcomes," "effects," or "results."</note> that are determined by them. The **law of gravitation** is different from the **law of cohesion**, insofar as the former refers to noticeable distances between particles, while the latter refers to the proximity of contact <note>Fechner is distinguishing between gravity, which acts over vast distances, and cohesion, the force that holds atoms or molecules together in a solid.</note>; these are different circumstances, with which a different result is also connected; and the different law simply determines the result that varies according to the different circumstances, or the relationship between the two. The same applies to laws in the **mental realm** <note>original: *im Geistigen*. This refers to the psychological or spiritual domain as opposed to the physical.</note>. Therefore, more general laws of occurrence are not only those that formally encompass a larger circle of laws, but also—because this is connected to it—those that in reality encompass a larger circle of circumstances and results between which they establish the relationship. Consequently, the question of whether a most general law of occurrence exists naturally becomes the following: is there a law that encompasses all possible laws, and all possible circumstances and all possible results that can occur within the realm of occurrence?

We have established such a law in the proposition <unclear>sentence</unclear>: "whenever and wherever the same circumstances recur—and whatever these circumstances may be—the same results also recur; however, under different circumstances, other results occur."

Fundamentally, this is the self-evident concept of a formally and really most general law for

To leave no doubt regarding the meaning of the terms, I understand once and for all by **circumstances** all specifiable determinations of material or mental **existence** in **space** and **time**; only the absolute location in space and the specific point in time cannot be regarded as a circumstance or a determination of existence, since it only receives its character through that which exists within it. Our most general law encompasses both the organic and the inorganic in equal measure and scope. It is, in fact, only a special—though very broad—case of our most general law, which I express in the proposition that, insofar as the same circumstances recur in the organic realm as in the inorganic, the same results will also recur; and insofar as the circumstances are not the same, the results will not be the same. Experience <note>original: *Erfahrung*. This refers to empirical observation and experimental data.</note> confirms this proposition as far as it is available to us, and thus simultaneously confirms our law itself through one of its most general applications.

Thus, the eye functions optically according to the laws of the *camera obscura* <note>original: *camera obscura*. Latin for "dark chamber," an early optical device consisting of a box with a hole that projects an image; Fechner is comparing the eye's lens and retina to this mechanism.</note>, because and insofar as the conditions of its structure are those of a camera obscura; the vocal organ <note>original: *Stimmorgan*. Referring to the larynx and its associated parts.</note> produces tones according to the laws of wind instruments and vibrating bands <note>vocal cords</note>, because and insofar as the conditions of its structure are the same; the heart functions like a pressure pump <note>original: *Druckwerk*. A mechanical apparatus used to exert pressure or move fluids.</note>, because and insofar as it is structured as such; the limbs function like levers and pendulums, because and insofar as they are structured as such; and so it is in all cases. In contrast, the organic body creates substances that can be produced in no retort or crucible <note>original: *Retorte* and *Tiegel*. Standard laboratory glassware and containers used in 19th-century chemistry.</note>, because the body is structured quite differently from these; in the nervous system, processes take place that occur nowhere else, because no equivalent structures exist elsewhere.

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s defense of "empirical inferences" (conclusions based on experience). On the previous page, he was explaining that his law allows us to draw reliable conclusions even when things are not perfectly identical.</meta>

In this way, the differences between cases are made just as useful for drawing a conclusion as the similarities. Most <term>empirical fallacies</term> <note>original: *Erfahrungsfehlschlüsse*; errors in reasoning based on observation.</note> stem from a failure to consistently separate and maintain this dual perspective. The frequency of such fallacies is the reason why people usually attribute only a shaky certainty to empirical inferences, especially when compared to so-called <term>rational inferences</term> <note>original: *Vernunftschlüsse*; logical deductions, like mathematics or syllogisms.</note>, which rest upon the <term>Law of Contradiction</term> <note>The logical principle that something cannot be both true and not true at the same time and in the same sense.</note>.

In truth, however, empirical inferences possess a fundamental certainty that equals our own "highest law." This law holds the same significance for the realm of physical reality as the Law of Contradiction holds for the realm of abstract concepts. Just as the world of reason cannot tolerate a contradiction, the real world cannot tolerate a contradiction with what has already been established as fact. Of course, since our law is a law of experience, its broadest proof can only be sought within the broadest possible experience. Naturally, errors made while applying empirical inferences can no more be blamed on the principle itself than a logical error can be blamed on the principles of reason.

Furthermore, we should note that rational inferences—without the inclusion of empirical ones—cannot mean anything for reality, let alone possess validity within it. For example, I can indeed conclude: "All men are mortal; Gaius is a man; therefore, Gaius is mortal." However, the fact that "all men are mortal" is itself first a matter of <term>induction</term> and <term>analogy</term>. Without these, the entire conclusion would be built upon a void. Accordingly, one can assert that the certainty of every conclusion rests upon the...

The main difficulty of valid <term>empirical inferences</term> <note>original: *Erfahrungsschlüsse*; conclusions drawn from observation rather than pure logic.</note> lies in the fact that in complicated processes—and all processes are more or less complicated—it is not immediately clear which specific elements should be related to one another as cause and effect. In this respect, a single experience can certainly never be the definitive standard for judging subsequent experiences. Our supreme law cannot spare us any of this work, but merely provides the most general perspective for it.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the universal law that governs both matter and spirit, transitioning from the concept of causal necessity to the possibility of freedom and individual character within that law.</meta>

In this respect, according to the law, everything was free from the beginning; and everything is still free now, insofar as old circumstances do not repeat—which, however, they never fully do.

* Applying this specifically to the **freedom of man**, it can be said:

Every human being—considered as a unity of both the spiritual and physical sides—represents a particular arrangement of circumstances, uniquely situated within the general arrangement of circumstances. This occurs in a manner that never repeats quite the same way anywhere else, and this constitutes their **individual character**. Thus, while a person is indeed bound to think and act in the same way as others to the extent that the preceding circumstances of their inner self and their position in the world are the same...

### Addition 1. On the manifold use of the concept of freedom.

According to some, acting from internal reasons—from **self-determination**, without external **coercion**—is generally considered free action; in which case, to be consistent, even a **planetary system** <note>original: *Planctensystem*; the author uses the orbits of planets as a metaphor for a system that moves according to its own internal laws without being pushed by outside forces.</note> that purely determines its own movements would have to be called "free" in the execution of these movements. From this point of view, one might even identify freedom with <term>internal necessity</term> <note>original: *innerer Nöthigkeit*; the idea that an entity is "free" if it simply acts out its own nature, even if that nature makes its actions inevitable.</note>, insofar as one considers self-determination to be something inherent in the nature of the **subject** and manifesting necessarily according to the subject’s nature. 

Elsewhere, freedom is said to require the absence of any coercion—whether internal or external—and in extreme views, perhaps even the absence of reasons altogether. At other times, it is merely the absence of internal or external **obstacles** to action that is demanded for the "freedom of action," though this would not in itself exclude the possibility that this action arose from internal or external necessitating reasons. In other cases, it is an "undeterminable possibility" of various ways of acting that is counted as freedom; but this undeterminable possibility can relate partly to each individual case in particular, and partly to the...

### Addition 2. On the opposition between the deterministic and indeterministic views.

In general, the **deterministic** view asserts a thoroughgoing **necessity** <term>necessity</term> <note>In philosophy, "necessity" (Nothwendigkeit) implies that an event must happen exactly as it does because of preceding causes; it could not have happened any other way.</note> of all events. It suggests that the spiritual, moral, willing, and thinking realms behave no differently than the physical realm, which is the object of **natural science**; the laws may be different, or more difficult to grasp and track, but the necessity is the same. Everywhere, that which happens follows with necessity from the given reasons, and everywhere only one way of occurring is possible, which is determined by the nature of the reasons present at that moment. These reasons are, in turn, pre-determined by the reasons lying behind them, and so on into infinity. If the internal and external nature of a human being were given, and the external circumstances were given, then everything would be given for them for eternity, as all consequences would develop with necessity into infinity according to these reasons. If a person believes they are acting freely, they are simply unaware of the compelling reasons.

The **indeterministic** view, as the opposite of the deterministic one, denies this thoroughgoing necessity, without being able or willing to deny that there is a realm or an aspect of necessity in the world. Its essence lies precisely in the fact that it does not deter- <note>The text cuts off here mid-word; the original German "bestimmt" likely means "determine" or "define."</note>

The idea of the existence of such a mediating medium is already found in the idea of the ubiquitous **electrical fluid**."

In addition, Weber expresses it as not improbable that the ubiquitous electrically neutral medium "coincides with the ubiquitous **ether**, which creates and propagates **light vibrations**."

If we base ourselves on the prerequisite of such a connection, which reaches through the whole world—even if only mediated through the **imponderable** <term>Unwägbare: things like light, heat, or electricity that were historically thought to lack physical weight.</term>—into which every individual organism must then also be integrated, then it is easy to see how considerations applicable to phenomena depending on **persistence** <note>Beharrung: often refers to inertia, the tendency of an object to remain in its state of rest or motion.</note>, **impact**, and **gravity** become inapplicable to everything that depends on this connection, and how the necessity that takes place in the realm of those phenomena is non-transferable to the realm of what depends on this connection.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the limits of human knowledge and the predictability of the future. The previous page established that a being cannot foresee events belonging to a higher stage of development than its own. Here, the author explores why the future must remain "indeterminable" to us and transitions into the practical implications for the debate between free will (indeterminism) and necessity (determinism).</meta>

Since the world is understood to be in a state of progressive development, we must confess that, for this reason as well, there exists an absolute impossibility in the very nature of the matter to calculate all the outcomes of the world in advance. This is because the calculation of that which will occur in a later, higher stage of development would already presuppose a being of that higher degree of development, which is a contradiction. And even if one wished to assert an objective calculability of everything that happens in the world in itself, this subjective uncalculability would always remain inherent in the nature of the matter.

One could indeed say that, although the knowledge of the future in this way always includes an element of indetermination <term>Indetermination: the philosophical concept that events are not strictly determined by prior causes and thus cannot be fully predicted</term>, it will, on the other hand, be possible for an attained higher level of knowledge to calculate the necessity of the earlier course of development <term>Bildungsgang: the path of formation, growth, or evolutionary progress</term> more and more in retrospect. However, if we look closer, it seems more accurate to express it this way: with an increasing degree of development, we become more and more capable of calculating what is necessary within a higher course of development; at least according to experience, we cannot assert anything else.

[necessary] **Determination** <term>Bestimmtheit: here referring to the fixed certainty or state of being destined to a specific path</term> if he only at the same time believes in the **Necessity** <term>Nothwendigkeit: the philosophical concept that things must happen as they do because of prior causes</term> of these consequences; in that case, the contemplation of them will necessarily co-determine him toward seeking to avoid them. The fact that the belief in this necessity is awakened in him lies within the necessity of the **World Order** <term>Weltordnung: the rational and moral structure of the universe</term> itself. 

If I do not tell him such things, others will tell him; if others do not tell him, he will see the consequences in others himself. And if all this telling and seeing yields no fruit—if the impulse of future consequences is not enough to enforce improvement—then the consequences that eventually truly occur will themselves finally be sufficient. The torment can and will ultimately always rise so high that it forces the person, first of all, to do everything to be rid of it, and then to avoid everything that could bring it about again. 

Generally, the stronger the conviction becomes—through any of these paths—that the consequences of evil will by necessity strike back at the evildoer himself and force him to change, the more the contemplation of these consequences will compel him to change right now. The fact that someone believes he is necessarily determined cannot, after all, cancel out the effect of the compelling determinations themselves; and yet, this always seems to be presupposed when one makes practical reproaches against **Determinism**. 

There exist, once and for all, compelling determinations toward the Good in the **World Order**, and indeed they are of such a nature that even the reflection upon this compulsion contributes to the compulsion itself. The deterministic faith, when understood correctly and thoroughly, thus belongs itself among the most effective **Means of Compulsion** <term>Nöthigungsmittel: the psychological or moral forces that "push" a person toward a certain behavior</term> toward the Good.

<meta>This page continues the argument from page 306, where the author began critiquing common misconceptions of indeterminism. ...the whole person as they have been up to now? According to common **indeterminism** <note>the philosophical doctrine that human choices are not determined by prior causes</note>, however, none of this plays a role in determining the will, insofar as it is free; and yet the most essential quality of the will is said to lie in its freedom. The point of this view is precisely to detach the will, in its free aspect, from this **causality** <note>the relationship between cause and effect</note>, and thereby from the person themselves. Thus, the free will hovers like a strange, uncanny power over everything that the person is and everything that acts upon them.

The free decisions of the will—on which, according to the prevailing indeterminist view, the most important matters for a human being are supposed to depend—basically bear the character of pure <term>contingency: (Zufälligkeit) the quality of happening by chance rather than by necessity or design</term>, since no prior or general reason is allowed to explain why the will decides for good rather than for evil. Granted, proponents attempt to reject this accusation of randomness by saying: the will establishes its own reasons, its own <term>motives: (Motive) the internal reasons or goals that drive an action</term>; this or that may present itself from the outside as a stimulus, but whether the will chooses to accept it as a motive is entirely up to the will itself. So long as it acts according to self-created or self-chosen motives, it does not act randomly.

This may be correct; the person's actions might then no longer be called random, but their *decisions of the will*—and this is what matters—still are. In this way, one only shifts the randomness from the action into the very core of the will itself; for it remains purely accidental why the free person adopts this and no other as a motive, or accepts it as a motive, because no <term>determining factor: (Bestimmungsgrund) a cause or logical basis that necessitates a specific outcome</term> connected to anything else is permitted to favor one choice over the other.

Now, it cannot be denied that, despite everything that can be said against the common ways of understanding indeterminism and in favor of the above view of **determinism**, there is nevertheless something in us...

This happens whenever we contrast the mental and physical aspects of a being: we imagine that which perceives itself from an *internal standpoint* being viewed simultaneously from an *external standpoint*. 2) that it is nonetheless inferred from the context of the experienced and according to rules that prove themselves in experience; 

3) that its assumption, while supplementing our field of experience without contradiction, does not come into conflict with our practical interests, but rather enters into them compatibly or productively.

There is much in the physical and psychical realms that can be thought of as an abstraction, but does not exist in such an abstract way—for example, speed, number, force, change, diversity, unity, order, and all general categories of reality in general. Thus, the bodies of spiritually high-standing individuals are made of the same material as those of spiritually lower-standing ones; human bodies are made of the same material as those of animals. <meta>This page continues Fechner’s mathematical analogy for the mind-body relationship. He is arguing against the idea that mental changes can occur without physical ones, using the concept of numerical series to show that the "soul" is essentially the internal mathematical relationship of the "body's" external states.</meta>
