To relate this schema to our general view of the relationship between **mind and body**, it would be incorrect to view the visible **physical numerical series** as the independent, substantial **fundamental essence**, and the invisible **ratio numbers** as a mere internal appearance dependent upon it; that would be entirely materialistic. <note>Fechner is critiquing "reductive materialism," which claims only the physical is real and the mental is just a shadow or byproduct.</note> In reality, the differences of the **base series** are just as much real numbers—though externally invisible and of a different nature—as the numbers of the base series themselves. Furthermore, the physical base series can just as easily be considered a function of the **mental difference series** <term>Differenzreihe: A mathematical series created by calculating the differences between terms in another series; Fechner uses this to symbolize how the mind represents the "rhythm" or "relationship" of physical states.</term> as the reverse.

Nor can one frame it as if the physical base series and the corresponding mental difference series (including any higher differences it might contain) were two inherently distinct things standing in a relationship of independence from one another, where the first is gifted only with the capacity to appear to others, and the second only with the capacity for **self-appearance** <note>original: "Selbsterscheinung," referring to subjective conscious experience.</note>. Instead, their difference depends solely on the fact that one and the same fundamental essence—which in reality is not separable at all—appears in one instance to someone other than itself in the form of the physical base series, and in the other instance to itself in the form of the mental difference series. In the first case, the **mode of appearance** is essentially determined by the relationship of the appearing fundamental essence to something external—relationships which do not concern the self-appearance as such. In the latter case, it is determined by the essence's own internal relationships, which again do not affect the appearance to others as such, even though both types of relationships change in **mutual interdependence**. Hence the appearance of different numbers in both series, insofar as numbers always serve to express relationships; but hence also their continuous connection.

The nature of an "Other" as well as the "Self" essentially enters into the **physical mode of appearance**; for it changes just as significantly according to the nature of the Other as it does according to the nature of the Self. <note>Fechner means that how my body appears depends not just on me, but on the senses and perspective of the person looking at me.</note> And so, according to our view, it can do no harm if one continues to regard **soul** and **body**, as is customary, as two different, interconnected sides of the same being, since the circumstance that the same being permits a two-sidedly different perception—from the **inside** and from the **outside**—can itself be seen as a two-sidedness of its nature. 

Indeed, one can even grasp them as something opposing, only we have now become aware that it is merely an opposition of the **point of view** from which they appear, and a difference in the beings to whom they appear, not an opposition in or to the **substance** <term>Substanz: In philosophy, the "stuff" things are made of. Fechner argues there is only one substance, appearing in two ways.</term> of the being itself that appears, which is what is at issue here as the basis for the different appearances.

Opposed to the fundamental or overly sharp division of the **physical** and the **spiritual** <note>original: "das Materielle und Geistige." I believe, however, that material nature can never be understood as a system of thoughts, and thought can never be understood as matter. <meta>This page continues the discussion regarding the nature of physical matter and thought. ...in a similar way, call it a function of the brain, just as the secretion of bile is a function of the liver. This may perhaps seem to amount to the same thing in practice; but a far-reaching clarity depends entirely upon the clear distinction between what belongs to two different viewpoints <note>The author is likely referring to the "dual-aspect" or "identity" view, where the mind and body are the same thing viewed from two different perspectives: the internal (mind) and the external (matter).</note>.

Common opinion has various expressions for the relationship between body and soul, such as that the body is the **carrier**, **support**, **seat**, **shell**, **organ**, or **condition** of the soul. We will still be able to use these expressions without danger, gaining the advantage of staying in touch with common understanding when explaining factual relationships—provided we always understand them in the sense of our fundamental view, or, if necessary, translate them into terms that refer back to it more directly.

The **carrier**, **support**, or **seat** of the spiritual is that physical thing whose state and changes are interdependent with those of the spiritual, or whose external appearance belongs to the **self-appearance** <term>self-appearance: (German: Selbsterscheinung) A philosophical term describing how a being experiences its own existence from within, such as consciousness or thought.</term> of the spiritual. <meta>This page continues Fechner’s argument that the confusion between the roles of the psychologist and the physiologist stems from a failure to recognize that they are looking at the same reality from different sides. He is transitioning into his famous "identity hypothesis"—the idea that the mental and physical are two aspects of one underlying unity.</meta>

But the psychologist, in his discussion of the **mental workings** <note>original: "geistigen Getriebes"; literally the "gears" or machinery of the mind.</note>, believes he must also take the physical into account—partly as **ballast** <note>In this context, things that weigh down or inhibit mental activity.</note>, partly as a **lever** <note>Things that provide a mechanical advantage or drive mental movement forward.</note> for mental movement. He believes he can explain many things through the physical that would otherwise be unexplainable, despite the fact that, from his own **standpoint** <term>standpoint: the specific perspective—either internal or external—from which a subject observes reality</term>, the task should be to seek the reasons for the internal inhibition or promotion of the mental only within the mental realm itself.

It is not that the physiologist should not consider the moving spirit, nor that the psychologist should ignore the externally stimulating nature and the person's own physical organs; no branch of knowledge can or should isolate itself so much from the others that it forgets its connections to them. However, these should then only be **points of connection** <note>original: "Anknüpfungspuncte"</note> to the other fields, not the specific bonds or the actual content of the teaching itself. But according to our view, the natural scientist as such no longer needs to tolerate the interference of mental principles into the field he treats, nor does he need to overstep into the mental field himself. 

Natural science can now enjoy a full internal consistency; it now receives the justification to coincide with the purest **materialism** <term>materialism: the philosophical view that everything, including thought and consciousness, results from physical interactions of matter</term>. Natural science has always shown a tendency toward this view, though it never quite dared to follow it, nor was it ever permitted to do so. Indeed, such permission could not be granted as long as mind and body seemed to struggle over the same territory—territory upon which, according to our view, they are now reconciled. Now we know that while natural science does provide the whole, it provides it only from one side, from one standpoint, and what...

Through the **confusion of standpoints**, however, the **common view** is characterized—for that is what I would like to call it—meaning the prevailing view unclearly mixed with philosophical ideas (to be distinguished strictly from the naturally alternating as well as the original spontaneous view); and one must unfortunately add that this also applies to many a philosophical view where viewpoints belonging to actually different modes of observation are unclearly mixed.

3) The **linking** (**natural-philosophical**) view, where one, combining both standpoints, follows the material and ideal sides in a consistent relationship to one another.

4) The **alternating** (**natural**) view, where one, changing the standpoint, goes back and forth between the material and ideal sides; it is to be called "natural" insofar as the change of standpoint in observation happens without reflection, in accordance with the natural position of the observer or according to analogies that assert themselves unconsciously.

The **common view** wavers unclearly back and forth between the others.

On the whole, I believe that through these six modes of observation, the possible cases for the underlying perspective of their distinction are exhausted: **always external**, **always internal** standpoint, **combination** of both, **alternating** between both, **identification** of both, **mixing** and **confusion** of both.

### c) Justification and Verification.

In the final analysis, we can view the entire preceding perspective as a generalized expression of **experience**, indeed, in a certain sense, merely as an explanation of **linguistic usage**.

In the first sense, we say: it is a general fact of experience that when we perceive something as **bodily**, **material**, **corporeal**, or **physical**, we find ourselves positioned against it from an **external standpoint**—either entirely or through a specific organ adapted for perception—whether in actual reality or in our imagination. If, however, we perceive it as **mental** or **psychic**, we are on the **internal standpoint** of <term>self-appearance (Selbsterscheinung; the way a being perceives its own existence from within)</term>.

In the latter regard, we say: one calls something bodily, material, corporeal, physical, or mental and psychic depending on whether it appears to another or appears to itself. However, even these latter expressions—"appearing to oneself" and "appearing to others"—must, according to linguistic usage, be related back to experiences. Certainly, a certain stabilization <note>original: *Fixirung*; here meaning a precise definition or standardization of terms</note> of linguistic usage, which otherwise allows for various turns of phrase, is necessary for scientific <term>consistency (Consequenz; the logical follow-through of a theory)</term>.

One might say: even if, in the sense of experience and linguistic usage, the mental (as that which appears to itself) is contrasted with the material (as that which appears to another), it does not follow that it is the same essence that appears to itself and that appears—or can appear—to another as something other than itself. It could well be that there is one being endowed with the capacity for self-appearance, and another which has the capacity...

### *Supplement 1. On the Closer Physiological Conditions of Objective Physical Appearance.*

We must carefully distinguish the **objective physical appearance**—which allows us to assume something physical exists beyond our perception of it, whereby a person standing before us, or our own hand or leg, appears as something existing independently of our perception—from mere **subjective physical feelings** (<term>general sensations (Gemeingefühle; the internal, non-localized feelings of one's own bodily state)</term>), such as pain, well-being, hunger, thirst, heaviness, effort, weakness, frost, or heat. While these may remind us that we have a body, they do not bring that body into objective appearance for us. Indeed, if we had not otherwise seen and felt the body externally through the eye and the <term>sense of touch (Getast; the active tactile system)</term>, we would never come to attach the idea of a body existing outside those feelings to the feelings themselves. We would always have only subjective, physical feelings or sensations, but not the idea of a body external to the **soul**. Yet it is this very idea that is at stake in the contrast between body and soul—a contrast that is different from the one between sensory feeling, sensory sensation, and higher spirituality, for the former, as such, still always belong to the soul. <note>The author argues that internal feelings like hunger or pain are "mental" experiences (belonging to the soul) and only become "physical objects" to us because we have sight and touch to verify them as things in space.</note>

Neither the nervous system alone nor the rest of the body alone would be able to produce them. However, for the emergence of the **objective appearance** of the physical or corporeal—by which it appears as something external in relation to the spiritual interior—the juxtaposition of body parts must fulfill special conditions. These conditions are actually met in the juxtaposition of the external sensory organs against the rest of the body and nature, and a thorough exami—

Accordingly, the viewpoint becomes an **external point of view**, which allows the **body** to appear as something objective, external to the **soul**; it must also everywhere demand the fulfillment of these or equivalent conditions (to be discussed in more detail shortly). Where there has been talk of an external viewpoint and of physicality in contrast to the spirit, the fulfillment of such conditions must always be silently presupposed.

What are these conditions? They can indeed be specified*. The following observation can lead us to them:

If we, looking out into a landscape, turn our head or eye, or touch an object with our finger, the **visual sensation** or **tactile sensation** changes in connection with our movement. When we have a headache or hunger, these sensations do not change in connection with our movement. They move along with us unchanged as we move; and thus we count them as part of ourselves—the one who is moving—and we do not set them in opposition to ourselves or attribute to them any cause that stands against us. On the other hand, those first sensations are objectified, or interpreted as if they depend on external objects, in relation to which we move and which we then characterize through these sensations themselves.

Admittedly, I also objectify a smooth mirror surface over which I run my finger, despite the fact that the tactile sensation does not change during this action; just as I do with a bird that flies past while my eye is held still, where a change in sensation occurs without my movement. A strict boundary between purely subjective bodily feelings or sensations and the objective appearance of the physical world cannot be drawn, however, precisely because these conditions of movement and sensation can be met in varying degrees of closeness.

### Supplement 2. Short Exposition of a New Principle of Mathematical Psychology.

For reasons whose discussion would lead too far afield here, I consider Herbart’s <note>Johann Friedrich Herbart (1776–1841) was a pioneer in psychology who believed that mental processes could be described mathematically, though he lacked an experimental method to prove it.</note> principle of mathematical psychology to be invalid. If such a thing is possible at all—and I believe that it is—it will, in my view, have to be based on taking the material phenomena, to which the mental ones are linked, as the foundation of the calculation. This is because these material phenomena allow for a direct point of application for calculation and a definite measure, which is not the case regarding mental phenomena. Although, in itself, nothing prevents us from viewing the material phenomena underlying given mental ones as a function of the mental, just as well as the reverse.

In any case, it is more valid to characterize the "measure of feeling" <note>original: "Gefühlsmaß"</note>—which is indisputable in itself but always imprecise—through a relationship to the more definite measure of the corresponding physical phenomena. This relationship should hold true everywhere within the limits of that measurement's certainty. By doing so, we indirectly raise the mental measure to a level of definiteness, rather than proceeding in the opposite direction and making the definite dependent on the imprecise.

For this, however, it is necessary that we no longer merely state the basic relationship between the physical and the mental in general terms—as has happened in previous considerations where the goal was only to establish the most general perspective—but that we also provide a specific mathematical relationship of dependence between them. In the absence of direct, precise measurability of phenomena in the mental field, this relationship must still lend itself to empirical verification for <term>limit cases (Gränzfälle): boundary conditions where a sensation begins or disappears, such as the threshold of hearing or sight</term>, changes and turning points, increases and decreases, the dominance and submission, or the superiority and subordination of spiritual phenomena. All of these things, even without precise measurement, can nonetheless be judged accurately by feeling or within consciousness. Furthermore, the calculation based on the principle of this dependence must be able to bring the quality of spiritual phenomena into its scope, in a sense similar to how <term>mathematical physics (rechnende Physik): the use of mathematical models to describe physical laws, such as the vibration frequencies of sound</term> has brought the quality of colors and tones into its scope, and indeed in a related manner. This would then also provide a firm scientific foundation for the entire fourth

<summary>Fechner proposes a new "mathematical psychology" (later known as psychophysics) which argues that since the mind cannot be measured directly, we must measure the physical stimuli that trigger mental sensations to create a precise scientific scale.</summary>

I believe, in fact, that I have found such a relationship of dependency which, at least as far as the matter can be judged so far, satisfies these requirements. It is as follows:

If we measure the strength of the **physical activity** that underlies a **mental** one, at a given place and a given time, by its **kinetic energy** $\beta$ <note>original: "lebendige Kraft." In 19th-century physics, this term (literally "living force") referred to what we now call kinetic energy, specifically $mv^2$.</note> (understanding kinetic energy in the mechanical sense \*), and we call the change of this energy—whether in an infinitely small part of space or time—$d\beta$, then the corresponding change in the **intensity of mental activity**—which is estimated by feeling or in consciousness—is proportional not to the **absolute** change of the kinetic energy $d\beta$, but to the **proportional** change $\frac{d \beta}{\beta}$. Thus, it can be expressed by $\frac{k d \beta}{\beta}$, or if we set $k$ once and for all = 1, by $\frac{d \beta}{\beta}$ itself.

If the kinetic energy of a material element is given at a specific time and place, one can arrive at the kinetic energy of any other element (or even the same element) in any other space and time by summing a continuous series of absolute increases. However, by performing the corresponding summation of the associated proportional increases—that is, through the **integral** <term>integral: a mathematical method for calculating the total value of something that is constantly changing, such as the total buildup of sensation from many tiny physical stimuli.</term>

->$\int \frac{d \beta}{\beta} \dots \dots (1)$<-

Insofar as the pitch of tones allows for a similar gradation as their strength, the soul performs this comparison according to the same principle as that of strength. Experience shows that perceived pitch is not determined by the inverse ratio of the duration of oscillation or the direct ratio of the number of oscillations <term>frequency: the number of vibrations per second</term>, but rather according to the logarithm of this ratio. The first and second octaves above the fundamental tone do not appear to us to be respectively twice or four times as high as the fundamental, despite the fact that the frequency is twice and four times as large; rather, the testimony of our feeling is that each octave is separated from the other by an equal interval, which corresponds to the logarithmic relationship. <meta>This page continues the technical exploration of how physical oscillations—such as sound waves and light waves—are summed by the mind to create sensations. It focuses specifically on the concept of "discontinuity" as the trigger for perceiving differences in intensity and quality.</meta>

A given interval of time and space is obtained through the summation of the sums belonging to the individual oscillations. Since, in the case of tones of different pitches and lights of different colors, the partial sums belonging to the individual oscillations differ not only because of the intensity of the movement but also due to the duration of the periods, the difficulty in comparing the intensity of tones of different pitches and lights of different colors in sensation undeniably depends on this, insofar as the comparison becomes more complex. If, however, a discontinuity in $\frac{d\beta}{\beta}$ <note>In psychophysics, this mathematical ratio often represents the relative change in a physical stimulus, such as energy or intensity.</note> and thus in $\gamma$ <note>Likely representing the magnitude of the resulting sensation.</note> occurs, a difference in intensity is perceived. Thus, when a second tone—even an identical one—is struck in addition to an existing tone, the new oscillation combines with the previous one; $\beta$ and $\gamma$ suddenly take on a different value, and we feel the difference in intensity *.

<meta>This page continues the author's exploration of a wave-based model of consciousness. Having previously established that consciousness can be visualized as a "main wave" of energy with smaller "ripples" representing specific sensations, the author now applies this model to explain everyday psychological experiences, such as the difference between distraction and the perception of absence (like silence or darkness).</meta>

This provides the possibility, or at least the foresight of a possibility, to represent many important psychological relationships.

For example, it explains the difference between *seeing nothing* because our attention is not occupied with visible things—even though light is striking our eye—and *seeing black*, a sensation that can be very intense even though it corresponds to a lack of light stimulation. We *see nothing* in the first sense when the main wave of kinetic energy <term>kinetic energy: German "lebendige Kraft" (vis viva). In this context, it refers to the physiological "driving force" or energy of the nervous system.</term> and its associated consciousness—which belongs to our visual organ as a member of an ensouled whole, independent of external stimuli—is below the threshold of consciousness. Even if ripples are present on that wave due to the influence of light, they are pulled down below the threshold of our general consciousness along with it. We *see black* when the main wave is above the threshold—and the higher it goes, the more intense the sensation—but there are no ripples caused by light stimulation upon it.

This principle can be applied to the other senses. Thus, we can distinguish *hearing nothing* due to withdrawn attention and feeling, from *silence*, when attention is awake in the realm of hearing but no stimulation from sounds occurs. It also effectively explains the common case where we might *physically* hear someone speaking but do not immediately *psychically* perceive it. We are, however, able to do so retroactively if we subsequently direct our attention to what was heard; by doing so, we lift the kinetic energy wave of the internal activity of hearing—along with the ripples awakened upon it, which were initially below the threshold—above the threshold *.

In general, this principle allows for many applications. For instance:

The reinforcement of the main wave through attention would then have to raise all tone waves above the threshold of consciousness to the same degree. On the other hand, the difficulty disappears if one assumes that the division of the auditory nerve into fibers (which is indeed difficult to interpret teleologically <note>Teleology is the study of purpose or design in nature. ## XX. Overview of the Doctrine of the Things of Heaven *.

1) In the sense of the intrinsically valid—if not common—way of viewing the Earth, which allows everything to be reckoned as part of it that is held together by <term>gravity: <note>original: "Schwere"</note> the force that pulls objects toward a center</term> around its center (thus including water, air, humans, animals, and plants) (II), the Earth represents a system. Just as much as our own body, it is a system intimately linked through the continuity of matter as well as in its purposes and effects. This system organizes itself into a variety of particularly distinguishable regions and parts, and unfolds a never-resting play of activities. This play is itself organized into a variety of periods and cycles and passes through great <term>epochs of development: <note>original: "Entwicklungsepochen"</note> significant historical or geological stages of growth</term>. Into this vast organization of parts and activities, our own body and its functions enter only in a subordinate manner (III, XV, B. ff.).

10) The supreme **world-law** (XI, B. XIX, B), the relationships between **necessity and freedom** (XI, B. XIX, B, C.), the relationships between **body and soul** (XI, p. 410. XIX, D.), and the manner in which **creatures** originate (XVI) are discussed in more detail from general perspectives.
